column16: The city of Atlanta accounts for 59 percent of State's economic output despite making up only 4.8 percent of the State's population. Globally, the city's economy is equally impressive, ranking 10th in U.S cities in the world economy with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of approximately $295 billion. Among the 12 largest U.S. metropolitan regions, Atlanta exhibited the fastest employment growth in 2016 with the addition of 75,000 jobs. The entertainment industry plays a major role in Atlanta's economy. In 2016, Georgia was the number one state in the U.S. for feature film production. As a result, the film industry has generated thousands of jobs and $6 billion for Georgia's economy in FY 2015 with an estimated 75-80 percent of productions filmed in the city. The music industry similarly has a significant impact on the both the culture and economy of Atlanta, contributing $3.7 billion in economic impact annually. Another asset critical to Atlanta's economy is the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is 10th in North America in cargo volume and generates $34.8 billion in economic activity. The Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport has been ranked as the world's most traveled airport by passenger traffic every year since 2000 and is considered a major hub for travel throughout the southeastern U.S. The Airport also provides more than 63,000 jobs on site, making it the state's largest employer. Despite Atlanta's array of economic assets and recent economic growth, Atlanta has the highest income inequality of any city in the U.S. and has continued to grow more unequal over the past decade. In 2014, the poorest 20 percent of households in Atlanta earned less than $15,000 annually, while the richest 5 percent of households in Atlanta earned more than $288,000. As the gap grows between rich and poor in the city, the middle class is shrinking. Compared to 50 other cities, Atlanta has the sixth lowest middle-class population (i.e. households with $40,000-$100,000 incomes), representing 32 percent of the population.

column16: Atlanta's economy and housing market was hit hard by the 2008 housing crisis. Since then, however, the city's housing market has recovered and is currently experiencing a wave of development and investment. Between 2000 and 2014, the city added nearly 40,000 new residential units, which grew the city's housing stock by 21.3 percent. More than 80 percent of these new units are part of multi-unit developments. Although increased development is a boon for Atlanta's economy, there is growing concern that it has had an adverse effect on affordability. A 2015 study by a real estate research firm found that from 2012-2014, 95 percent of apartments built in Atlanta were classified as luxury rentals. The study also found that the average rent in the city rose from $1.62 to $1.74 per square foot, or 7 percent, between 2015 and 2016. Simultaneously, the number of low-cost rental units (less than $750 a month) is declining by 4.4 percent per year. As a result of new higher-end development and an overall increase in cost of living, coupled with below national average household income, 16 percent of renters and homeowners are cost burdened by their housing situation and are housing insecure — spending at least half their income on housing costs. More specifically, 26 percent of renters are extremely cost burdened (spending more than 50 percent of their income on housing costs), indicating that renters are especially vulnerable to changes in the housing market. Since 2009, the number of extremely cost burdened renters has steadily increased. Despite the need for more affordable housing, Atlanta has a high vacant property rate at nearly 20 percent (reaching up to 40 percent in some neighborhoods), which increased by two percent between 2010 and 2014. These vacant properties are largely concentrated in the south and west areas of the city, which struggle with blight and are especially vulnerable to gentrification forces as the Atlanta BeltLine plans to extend into these neighborhoods.

column16: Both the city and region have experienced significant growth over the last decade. The city's population increased by 12 percent from 2010 to 2016, reaching 473,000 in 2016. This increase is slightly higher than that of the 29-county Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA), which grew 10 percent over the same time period. Net domestic in-migration has played a major role in the City's population growth as more millennials and middle income Americans move to lower cost Sun Belt cities like Atlanta. The Atlanta Regional Commission estimates that by 2040 the wider 20-county Atlanta region will add 2.5 million people and 1 million jobs, increasing from 5.6 million to 8.0 million people and from 2.9 million to 3.9 million jobs. Atlanta is among the most ethnically integrated cities in the U.S. Data released by the Pew Research Center indicates that 78 counties nationwide experienced a switch in majority minority population since 2000 and four of these counties are located in the Atlanta region. The city's recent population growth, however, has spurred changing demographics. From 2000-2016 the percentage of city residents who identify as either White or Asian increased by 7 percentage points and the percentage of African American residents decreased by 9 percentage points. Furthermore, the region remains largely divided along racial lines with the White population clustered in the north and the Black population clustered in the south. With this rapid population growth, coupled with expanding income inequality and numerous high-end real estate investments, Metro Atlanta is at risk of becoming an increasingly divided region - racially, socially, and geographically. Atlanta's vibrant culture and history and its role in the Civil Rights movement are two of its most unifying traits; yet, if these qualities are not preserved and strengthened, the city could lose part of its tangible heritage. There is a need now more than ever to empower residents to strengthen community roots, preserve Atlanta's history, and embrace a shared, multigenerational identity.

column16: In the past, Atlanta has normally experienced large amounts of rainfall, evenly spread through the year. However, as one of the few U.S. metropolitan areas not built around a major local body of water, the city is particularly vulnerable to drought. Exceptionally low amounts of rainfall in the region since 2007 have put increasing pressure on the city's water supply and recently caused Georgia's Environmental Protection Division to declare a Level 2 drought. A current project to repurpose the Bellwood Quarry as a 2.5 billion gallon reservoir will increase the city's reserve supply from just 3 days to 30 days in 2018. Reliability and access to water, however, will continue to be a resilience issue for Atlanta. In addition to drought, the city faces substantial risk from rainfall flooding. In September 2009, Atlanta experienced historic flash flooding, which resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in damages and the loss of at least ten lives. The flooding was so extreme that in one 24- hour period some counties in the region saw more than 20 inches of rain, conditions so rare that there is only a 0.01 percent chance of it happening each year. The severity of this flooding was, in part, attributed to increased concrete surfaces, overfilled sewers, and blocked storm drains. Today, the city and region continue to face periods of intense flooding. Finally, increasing temperatures and number of days with high temperatures pose a risk to Atlanta's residents and the environment. On average, across the country, cities are getting hotter faster than adjacent rural areas. Assuming greenhouse gas emission trends continue through 2100, within the next century Atlanta will be above 95 degrees Fahrenheit for more than three months per year. High temperatures are especially dangerous for infants and the elderly, and those living without access to air conditioning will be disproportionately impacted.

column16: Housing - Birmingham has a relatively old housing stock with many residential areas being built in the Victorian, Edwardian and inter-war periods. Consequently, many homes are over 70 years old and have inherent issues such as single-skin walls and poor quality original construction. Households living in properties built before 1919 had the highest average gap at £612 and the largest proportion of fuel poverty (17.1 per cent). A substantial number of more recent properties were built using non-traditional (system built) construction methods, which can require costly structural work. The Council owns a large number of these properties, with over 200 tower blocks, low rise flats and some houses. This type of housing is the least thermally efficient - Central Governments 'Help to heat' consultation identified that the most fuel poor in social housing live in this type of property. The most recent Birmingham Private Sector Stock Condition Survey (2010) found that 46,000 private sector homes failed on the thermal comfort criteria. Updated stock condition surveys are taking place between 2024-2028. The information gathered from the surveys will be used to help identify where improvement works are required and will be used to develop future programmes of work. There is also inadequate supply of homes to meet the needs of people especially shortage of homes for older people, people with specialist needs and people with dementia. Also densification of the city amplifies the urban heat island effect. Of all of the city's properties: 151,248 (33.4% of total dwellings) have an EPC of A-C and 302,147 (66.6% of total dwellings) are EPC D and below, with the most amount of dwellings are rated D (185,561) (40.9%).

column16: Climate migration has growing implications for Chicago's adaptive capacity. It both strengthens and strains the city's systems. As climate change drives displacement in other parts of the U.S. (and globally), cities like Chicago have seen an increase in migrants. The recent surge of asylum seekers—over 16,000 sent from border states like Texas—has overwhelmed city services, including shelters, schools, and healthcare. Chicago's role as a potential “climate haven” is both promising and complex. Climate migration could boost adaptive capacity by revitalizing neighborhoods and increasing resources—if it's managed with equity and foresight. Without proactive policies, however, it risks worsening existing vulnerabilities and straining underprepared systems.

The plan includes seven action areas, such as improving systems of care, transforming policies, and strengthening youth leadership. The Healthy Chicago Survey and Community Health Needs Assessment (CHNA) provide real-time data to guide interventions and track progress. CDPH collaborates with over 40 stakeholders to ensure that public health responses reflect community needs and strengths Chicago's public health system is both a pillar of resilience and a mirror of systemic challenges. Its adaptive capacity hinges on how well it can balance equity-driven innovation with the realities of limited resources and rising demand. The city's commitment to community-led planning and data transparency is a major strength.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Climate is taken into consideration through the London Plan, which has policies designed to drive down greenhouse gas emissions from new buildings, both in terms of construction materials and when the buildings are in use, and for adapting to climate change. The London Plan provides policies for dealing with flood risk and overheating risk, the implementation of sustainable drainage, as well as the management of water resources and water infrastructure to address water scarcity. The London Plan also takes consideration of climate in terms of ensuring new developments are well served by public transport, and it commits the Mayor to working with the Environment Agency and relevant local authorities including outside London to safeguard locations for a new Thames Barrier in the future (which is likely to be needed to protect the city from future climate related flood events). A Sustainability Statement has been made available that outlines and describes the environmental and sustainability considerations and the views of consultees that have been integrated into the London Plan 2021 (https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/london_plan_2021_sustainability_statement.pdf). The next London plan will be informed by the London Climate Resilience Review. The London Plan is currently undergoing a review and a new Plan will be adopted in 2027, setting out a framework for how London will develop until 2050.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Poverty means that people will have fewer resources to help them prepare, respond, or recover. It also means a greater likelihood of health problems and other factors of vulnerability. Poverty remains a real problem in London, with persistent poverty a particular issue for many individuals. The percentage of Londoners in poverty has decreased only marginally over twenty years and stands at 24 per cent. As the population has grown, this represents an increase in the number of people to 2.2 million. Around one in seven Londoners, including around one in five children, are in persistent poverty. The proportion of London's pensioners in material deprivation, at 12 per cent, is the highest among all the regions and countries in the UK, while Inner London has an even higher rate (20 per cent). Living in poverty is associated with poorer health, particularly cardiovascular and mental health - many of the health conditions with higher prevalence in the lowest decile groups are also climate sensitive health conditions.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: London is England's top region for outcomes at the end of primary and secondary school. However, there are still key challenges London faces across all age groups in education. London has lower free early years provision take-up rates for 2 year-olds than England (68% compared with 74%). 2023 data shows that 98% of early years children in schools attend a setting that is 'good' or 'outstanding'. In 2022-23, London had a higher percentage of pupils achieving a standard 9-4 pass in English and Mathematics (71%) than England (65%) for Key Stage 4. 80% of London's Asian pupils achieved a standard pass in 2022-23, compared to 66% of Black pupils, 68% of Mixed pupils, 70% of White pupils and 70% of Other pupils. London has among the fewest apprenticeship starts of any region in England: In 2022/23, there were 36,120 apprenticeship starts in London across all age groups, the fourth lowest of any region and the lowest per 1000 residents aged 16 to 64. Apprenticeship success rates in London are the lowest of any region in England: Level 2: London=65.9%; other regions=varies between 70.1%-73.0%. Level 3: London=68.3%; other regions=varies between 71.8%-76.0%.There is considerable variation in apprenticeship numbers by industry sector and by area of London.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Inequality in access to opportunities affects outcomes, including the ability of individuals and communities to adapt. Climate change will exacerbate existing inequalities, which means that vulnerable people will be even less able to prepare, respond, and recover, and potentially more people will be vulnerable. In London, this means that those who are already disadvantaged—such as individuals over 65, babies and young children, people with underlying health conditions, pregnant women, and those living in deprived areas—are at increased risk from climate impacts. Climate-sensitive health conditions, like cardiovascular disease and mental health issues, are more prevalent in deprived areas and among ethnic minority communities, exacerbating their vulnerability. People living in the most deprived areas, people from ethnic minority communities, and people already experiencing disadvantage are more likely to be exposed to high temperatures, cold temperatures, flooding, and food and water insecurity. Additionally, people facing disadvantage often lack the resources and opportunities needed to adapt, such as implementing adaptation measures or benefiting from urban greening projects.

Social dimensions of heat and flood vulnerability were explored in detail in research for the Joseph Rowntree Foundation's Climate Just programme. This research set out indicators of social vulnerability to these hazards - it's not as simple as the Index of Multiple Deprivation, because there are some factors that make people vulnerable specifically to heat or drought. We have applied these indicators to London as a whole, although recognize that there will be local variation, and therefore we can promote this approach with London boroughs and other partners to encourage them to use their local data and intelligence to understand their vulnerable populations better.

column16: London has a well-established public health system at both local and regional level. There is a London Climate and Health network and a London Climate and Health Advisory group. The city is also supported by the recently established Public Health Unit within the GLA, which was set up to embed a Health in all Policy approach across all GLA Group activities, including climate. The public health sector is crucial in ensuring population health, particularly ensuring that policy action within the city is equitable and directed to the greatest need. The London system is supported by the UK Health Security Agency which delivers the UKHSA Adverse Weather and Health Plan and associated early warning system for heat and cold, and carries out population level surveillance, including for vectors. Additionally, the GLA Public Health Unit's Hot Weather Severe Weather Emergency Protocol (H-SWEP), provides guidance for organisations providing support for rough sleepers in London to ensure that steps are taken to protect their health during extreme heat or cold A healthier population will be more resilient to climate impacts.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Infrastructure managers often point out that infrastructure resilience relies primarily on basic maintenance and upkeep of assets. In London, basic highways maintenance is stressed by declining budgets. Also, London's water distribution network is ageing and this can cause problems in addressing leakage, as the network is difficult and expensive to upgrade. Over recent years, considerable effort and investment has been made to reduce leakage rates and increase water efficiency. There has been some success, with reduced leakage rates across London between 2000 and 2015, and just over seven per cent reduction in per capita consumption over the same period. However, more recently, leakage targets in London have been missed and latest statistics indicate that loss due to leakage is increasing with an average of 24% of water lost. L. atest figures indicate this amounts to approximately 602 million litres per day as a result of leakage. https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2024-03/Water%20and%20London%27s%20rivers%20report.pdf

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Existing housing stock in London poses a challenge for both climate change mitigation and adaptation. Emissions reductions from housing stock will be required to mitigate climate change, and is being addressed through retrofit programmes for existing housing, and London Plan and other policies for new development. Housing must also be equipped to ensure safety and comfort in face of increasing climate impacts facing London - heat risk, flooding, and water scarcity. Ensuring that all of London's housing stock is equipped for expected climate changes is a challenge with further action needed. Quality of housing is particularly important in terms of vulnerability to heat risk. Being homeless is also a factor in vulnerability. Housing tenure and income are also factors - people who rent, for example, are less able to make changes to their properties to address risks. The proportion of owner-occupiers in London is 48%, compared with 65% in the rest of England. London households that are private renters spend a greater proportion of their income, including Housing Benefit, on rent (45%) compared with households outside London (32%). A similar picture exists for social renters (32% in London compared with 27% outside London).

National figures show that almost 13,000 homes in Newcastle suffer from fuel poverty and it's estimated that a further 10,000 are just above the current definition and only a small change in income levels could result in them being classed as fuel poor. Fuel poverty in England is now measured using the Low Income Low Energy Efficiency (LILEE) indicator , which considers a household to be fuel poor if: • it is living in a property with an energy efficiency rating of band D, E, F or G as determined by the most up-to-date Fuel Poverty Energy Efficiency Rating (FPEER) Methodology -and • its disposable income (income after housing costs (AHC) and energy needs) would be below the poverty line. Based on the latest methodology, the average fuel poverty figure across all Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs) in Newcastle is 16.37%. Evidence strongly suggests that fuel poverty leads to more people living in colder temperatures and are more likely to experience poorer physical and mental health because of this. Unemployment and impacts on household income arising from Covid-19 are expected to exacerbate these issues. column16: In terms of infrastructure capacity to manage flood risk, the Flood and Water Management Act 2010 required UK local authorities to lead co-ordination of flood risk management for groundwater, surface-water and ordinary (smaller) watercourses, and to develop local flood risk management strategies, under the designation of Lead Local Flood Authority. In line with this Reading Borough Council produced a Local Flood Risk Management Strategy in 2015. This identified 7 flood risk 'hotspots' and mitigation action required to reduce flood risk in these areas. Six of these projects have now been implemented and funding has been approved for the final, outstanding scheme. Options for this scheme are currently under review as the original proposals now appear unfeasible.The Borough Council also commissioned a Strategic Flood Risk Assessment (SFRA) in 2017 to inform development of the Reading Local Plan (adopted 2019), the strategic spatial plan for the area. Informed by the SFRA, Policy EN18 in the Local Plan sets out the framework for considering development proposals to reduce their exposure to flood risk by directing development to areas at lowest risk of flooding, taking into account the effects of climate change and requiring all new developments in areas of flood risk to give priority to Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems. The Plan is currently being reviewed and updated and climate adaptation policies are among those under review.

A high priority set by the Adaptation & resilience Team identifies the need to alter the course of rivers back to the way they were to reduce rates of flow and to store water thus reducing the rislk of flooding.

Climate change poses significant risks to urban ecosystems through increased 
temperatures, pollution, habitat degradation, and the spread of invasive species. These 
factors can lead to a decline in biodiversity and affect ecosystem services in Coventry, a 
city already facing challenges with green space availability and green deprivation.

While biodiversity is important, the focus should be on developing ecologically sensitive 
approaches that mimic natural ecosystems. This strategy can reduce the need for costly 
interventionist land management practices. By creating systems that are closer to natural 
ecosystems, we can enhance resilience against climate impacts such as heatwaves and 
flooding, while potentially improving air quality and providing recreational spaces.

In some cases, the use of non-native, climate-adapted species may be appropriate, 
particularly in areas facing heat stress and low water availability. These species can 
survive in challenging conditions and contribute to cooling urban areas.

Adapting to these risks will strengthen Coventry's resilience against climate impacts, 
potentially improve quality of life for residents, and create a more sustainable urban 
environment. This approach balances ecological considerations with practical, cost-effective solutions for climate adaptation.

These groups may face barriers to evacuation, health services, or adaptation measures due to language, mobility, or economic constraints.Cardiff has socio-economic inequalities between the north and south of the city, with the southern arc having the poorest quality housing, lowest incomes, lowest life expectancies etc.

Nearly one-fifth of Cardiff's Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs) are ranked among the most deprived in Wales - the third highest among Welsh local authorities. These communities are more vulnerable to climate hazards such as flooding, heatwaves, and infrastructure disruption due to:
- Poor housing quality (e.g. flats prone to overheating)
- Limited financial capacity to invest in resilience (e.g. flood-proofing, cooling systems)
- Reduced access to insurance and recovery resources

Within the deprived areas, Cardiff also has multiple neighbourhoods rated in the highest categories of the Neighbourhood Flood Vulnerability Index (NFVI) - especially in Ely and Rhymney catchments. As a result, the risk of the following increases:
- Greater likelihood of displacement
- Mental health stress due to financial loss and housing insecurity
- Strain on council services for temporary accommodation and recovery

The reliance on these sectors created challenges to the District's economy during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. As telework became more standardized, according to the DC Policy Center, “the District's share of workers in business and financial occupations in the metro region declined from 30 percent in 2019 to 21 percent post-pandemic. Prior to the pandemic, 54 percent of the region's lawyers worked in D.C. Post pandemic, that share is 37 percent. Between 2010 and 2018, the District experienced strong domestic in-migration, which brought nearly 30,000 residents to the city—mostly millennials—who then chose to stay in the city at historically high rates after they formed families and their children began to attend D.C.'s public schools. This influx of new residents contributed to growing resident employment, higher resident incomes, and higher income tax revenues for years to come. Between 2015 and 2021, the District's individual income tax revenue, adjusted for inflation, grew by 20 percent, nearly twice the pace of growth in real GDP across the Washington metropolitan area. In contrast, between 2020 and 2023, the city has lost 26,210 residents to net domestic outmigration. This has meant fewer families, fewer babies, and a lower demand for D.C.'s public schools. Many of those who left are higher income residents or residents with high income potential. High housing and childcare costs have always been factors driving families out of the city. Nonetheless, the declining importance of commute times post-pandemic made such a move easier and shifted demand for housing from the District to the outer suburbs of the Washington metropolitan area, which offer a lower cost of living and amenities valued by families.\n\nThe economy's reliance on the Federal government also revealed vulnerability during the 2013 government shutdown during which most Federal operations were suspended for 16 days. The City of Johannesburg faces persistently high unemployment rates, particularly among its youth population. In the fourth quarter of 2024, youth aged 15-24 years had an unemployment rate of 59.6%, while those aged 25-34 years had a rate of 39.4% . Furthermore, approximately 3.5 million young people aged 15-24 were not in employment, education, or training.
This high unemployment significantly challenges the city's ability to adapt to climate change because it limits the available skilled and motivated workforce needed to implement climate resilience initiatives. The “youth dividend,” which represents the potential economic and innovative contributions of young people, is diminished when large numbers remain unemployed or underemployed.
Without meaningful employment opportunities, young people may have fewer resources and incentives to participate in or support climate adaptation programs, reducing community resilience and the effectiveness of climate action. Additionally, unemployment exacerbates socio-economic vulnerabilities, making it harder for affected populations to recover from climate-related shocks and stresses.
Addressing youth unemployment is therefore critical not only for economic development but also for enhancing the city's adaptive capacity and achieving sustainable, inclusive climate resilience.

These fiscal constraints temporarily challenged the City's adaptive capacity by limiting immediate investments in infrastructure and climate resilience programmes.\nIn response, the City has implemented comprehensive social support packages aimed at mitigating the socio-economic impacts on vulnerable communities. These include emergency relief grants, expanded food security programmes, temporary housing support, and skills development initiatives targeted at unemployed residents. By cushioning vulnerable populations and promoting economic recovery, these social support measures strengthen the City's social adaptive capacity and help maintain community resilience.\n

The City's Final Adaptation Plan Review (2019) highlights that ageing and poorly maintained infrastructure poses a significant challenge to climate adaptation and directly undermines the City's adaptive capacity. Beyond water infrastructure—where approximately 40% of water is lost due to outdated systems—other critical infrastructure types are also highly vulnerable. Electrical grids, transport networks, and stormwater management systems are increasingly at risk from climate-related shocks such as flooding, heatwaves, and severe storms.
For instance, aging electrical infrastructure leads to frequent outages during extreme weather, disrupting essential services and economic activities. Transport infrastructure, including roads and bridges, is susceptible to damage and erosion during floods, limiting mobility and emergency response capabilities. Additionally, inadequate stormwater drainage exacerbates urban flooding, threatening low-income and vulnerable communities disproportionately.
These vulnerabilities increase the exposure and sensitivity of residents, especially those in informal settlements and other at-risk areas, to climate hazards. Without urgent and sustained investment to upgrade and maintain diverse infrastructure systems, the City's capacity to absorb, respond to, and recover from climate impacts remains severely constrained, limiting long-term resilience and adaptive capacity

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16:
Access to basic services is a critical factor influencing the adaptive capacity of Johannesburg. Despite efforts to improve service delivery, many residents—particularly those living in over 300 informal settlements—still face inadequate access to essential services such as clean water, sanitation, electricity, and waste management. This lack of reliable basic services severely compromises their quality of life and limits their ability to cope with and recover from climate-related shocks and stresses.
Insufficient access to clean water and sanitation increases vulnerability to health risks during extreme weather events, such as floods and heatwaves. Limited electricity access affects the ability to use cooling systems or preserve food during power outages, while inadequate waste management exacerbates environmental health hazards. The cumulative effect is heightened exposure and sensitivity among vulnerable communities, reducing the overall resilience of the City.
Improving access to basic services, especially in informal settlements, is therefore essential to strengthening social and physical adaptive capacity. Targeted interventions to upgrade service delivery help reduce vulnerability and build a more climate-resilient Johannesburg.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16:
Johannesburg, as South Africa's economic hub, exhibits high levels of inequality, with a Gini coefficient of approximately 0.65. This inequality is deeply rooted in historical and socio-economic factors, primarily characterized by race and spatial segregation. The spatial dimension manifests in the unequal distribution of resources, services, and opportunities across the city, with marginalized communities—often located in informal settlements and underserved areas—bearing the brunt of these disparities.
This entrenched inequality significantly challenges the City's adaptive capacity. Marginalized populations have limited access to financial resources, information, infrastructure, and social services necessary to effectively prepare for, respond to, and recover from climate change impacts. Structural barriers restrict their ability to implement adaptive measures, increasing their vulnerability to extreme weather events and long-term climate stresses.
Furthermore, inequality exacerbates social tensions and undermines social cohesion, which are critical components of community resilience. Addressing these inequalities is therefore essential to enhancing adaptive capacity and ensuring an inclusive, equitable approach to climate adaptation in Johannesburg.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16:
Johannesburg experiences an annual influx of approximately 3,000 new residents, significantly increasing demand for housing, infrastructure, and essential services. According to the City's latest Spatial Development Framework (SDF), rapid urbanisation continues to place immense pressure on existing urban areas, particularly as many new residents settle in informal settlements and environmentally vulnerable zones prone to flooding and other climate risks.
The SDF highlights that unplanned and fragmented urban growth exacerbates service delivery challenges and limits the City's capacity to implement integrated climate adaptation measures. Overburdened infrastructure networks, combined with spatial inequality, reduce the effectiveness of interventions aimed at improving resilience. Furthermore, the spatial mismatch between affordable housing, employment opportunities, and basic services reinforces socio-economic vulnerabilities, undermining adaptive capacity.
However, the SDF also outlines a strategic vision to manage urban growth more sustainably by promoting densification, mixed land use, and the development of climate-resilient infrastructure in priority areas. By aligning urban planning with climate adaptation objectives, the City aims to reduce exposure to hazards, improve service delivery, and enhance overall adaptive capacity.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16:
The City of Johannesburg faces significant socio-economic challenges, with an estimated poverty rate of 51% and youth unemployment at approximately 55%. These high levels of poverty constrain the adaptive capacity of individuals and communities by limiting their access to essential resources needed to withstand and recover from climate impacts.
Poverty in Johannesburg exacerbates food insecurity, which is a critical focus of the City's Food Resilience Policy. Many vulnerable households in the City struggle to access sufficient, affordable, and nutritious food, increasing their susceptibility to health and economic shocks caused by climate events such as droughts, floods, and extreme heat. The Food Resilience Policy highlights that food insecurity undermines household resilience by fostering dependence on unstable food supply chains and compromising nutritional health, thereby reducing the capacity for recovery and adaptive responses.
To address these challenges, the City is implementing targeted interventions outlined in the Food Resilience Policy. These include promoting urban agriculture and community food gardens, strengthening local food systems, and supporting food distribution initiatives that improve food access and create livelihoods. Special emphasis is placed on empowering marginalized groups, including youth and women, to participate in these initiatives, thus fostering economic opportunities alongside improved food security.
By integrating poverty alleviation efforts with food resilience strategies, the City aims to enhance social adaptive capacity, reduce vulnerabilities, and build more inclusive, climate-resilient communities capable of better coping with current and future climate challenges.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.

The post-apartheid legal framework in Johannesburg has established strong foundations for grassroots participation in government and governance processes. This framework mandates transparency in municipal business planning, including budgeting and infrastructure development, ensuring that these plans are developed collaboratively with communities. Such inclusivity enhances trust, accountability, and shared ownership of climate adaptation initiatives.
Public engagement mechanisms enable diverse community voices—especially those from vulnerable and marginalized groups—to be heard and integrated into decision-making. This participatory approach strengthens adaptive capacity by fostering local knowledge, enhancing awareness of climate risks, and encouraging community-led solutions.
Furthermore, climate actions in Johannesburg benefit from cross-governmental support, reinforced by legislation such as the recent Climate Change Act. This legal backing ensures alignment and coherence in adaptation efforts, while also promoting transparency and stakeholder collaboration.
Overall, this democratization of governance and transparency is a key enabler of community resilience, empowering citizens to actively participate in climate adaptation and enhancing the City's ability to respond effectively to climate challenges.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.

Access to quality and relevant data is a critical component of Johannesburg's adaptive capacity; however, data availability remains limited and unevenly utilized across the City. While technological advancements and increased mobile phone penetration have made data more accessible, many vulnerable communities still lack the means or capacity to effectively access and apply this information for climate adaptation.
This gap challenges adaptive capacity by restricting timely awareness of climate risks, early warning systems, and opportunities for proactive decision-making at the community level. Furthermore, data management and integration across different municipal departments are still evolving, which can delay comprehensive planning and response.
Nonetheless, the widespread use of cellular phones presents a significant opportunity to improve data dissemination and engagement, especially if tailored communication strategies are implemented to reach marginalized groups. Enhancing digital literacy and investing in inclusive data platforms could enable more communities to benefit from relevant climate information, thereby strengthening their ability to anticipate, prepare for, and respond to climate impacts.

Since its founding during the 1886 gold rush, Johannesburg has been a major destination for migrants both domestically and internationally, attracted by opportunities for economic prosperity. Migration continues to shape the City's demographic and socio-economic landscape, contributing to urban growth and diversity.
However, recent years have seen migration intensify social and economic pressures, exacerbated by the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. These pressures have sometimes sparked social unrest and tensions, leading to societal fragmentation. Such divisions undermine social cohesion, which is a vital component of community resilience and collective adaptive capacity.
The complexity of managing migration-related challenges—such as housing shortages, competition for resources, and service delivery backlogs—further complicates efforts to implement inclusive and effective climate adaptation strategies. Addressing migration-related social dynamics and fostering inclusive governance are therefore essential to strengthening Johannesburg's adaptive capacity in the face of climate change.

En Bogotá, por ejemplo el fenómeno de “La Niña” se asocia con el aumento de las precipitaciones, que traen como consecuencia el incremento de eventos climáticos extremos tales como deslizamientos de tierra e inundaciones, esto conlleva a la pérdida de cultivos que ocasionan escasez de alimentos que derivará en la inseguridad alimentaria y desnutrición en algunas comunidades. Así mismo estos fenómenos traen consigo la contaminación hídrica, haciendo que el agua limpia se junte con aguas negras, esto puede desencadenar en enfermedades gastrointestinales. Hong Kong is an international city, reliable water supply is essential to its daily operation and sustainable development. 
Currently, about 20-30% of freshwater water supply in Hong Kong comes from the local catchment and the remaining 70% to 80% is imported from Dongjiang (DJ) in Guangdong Province up to an annual supply ceiling of 820 million m3. Besides, 1,100 million m3 has been allocated and reserved for Hong Kong to meet its long term needs. 
The Water Supplies Department also supplies seawater for toilet flushing. Currently, it saves about 320 million m3 of freshwater every year. 
With this three-pronged water supply system, we should be able to maintain the reliability level of water supply in Hong Kong not lower than 99% in the short to medium term.
In the long-run, the water resources and security in Hong Kong face a number of uncertainties. Hong Kong currently has two freshwater sources, local yield and DJ water, both of which are vulnerable to climate change impacts. Another challenge is the continuous increase in water demand from population growth.
To better prepare Hong Kong for the aforesaid uncertainties (i.e. climate changes and persistent demand growth), the Hong Kong Government promulgated the Total Water Management Strategy (the Strategy) in 2008 mapping out the strategy for sustainable use of water to ensure water security and support the development in Hong Kong. We completed a review on the Strategy in 2019 and updated the Strategy which adopts a two-pronged approach, with emphasis on containing fresh water demand growth and building resilience in the fresh water supply catering for extreme effects of climate change with diversified water resources. The water management measures are as follows:
Water Conservation
We have been taking a multi-pronged approach to promote water conservation using both hardware and software measures, including Water Efficiency Labelling Scheme, automatic meter reading, free distribution of flow controllers to residents who have signed up e-Bills, public education, best practice guidelines for major water-consuming trades, etc.

Hong Kong's fresh water and salt water supplies are provided through a network of over 8 400 kilometres of water mains. After the substantial completion of the 15-year replacement and rehabilitation programme for 3,000-kilometres aged water mains in 2015, the healthiness of the water supply networks has been greatly improved. Owing to the hilly terrain of Hong Kong, in order to maintain adequate water supply pressure for premises located at high ground, the water pressure of the water supply networks in Hong Kong generally ranges from 60 metres to 80 metres, which is higher than that of other cities. In addition, the water supply networks in Hong Kong are mostly underground. The congested underground public utilities, busy traffic and frequent repairs of the public utilities and roadworks, etc. all cause vibration and disturbance to the underground water mains. Therefore, the timescale for the risk will be “Medium term”.

The above factors cause an increase in the risk of water mains bursts and leakage in the water supply networks in Hong Kong, which have caused inconvenience to the public and resulted in water loss.

Risk-based Water Main Asset Management
Following the substantial completion of the 15-year replacement and rehabilitation programme in 2015, the condition of the water distribution network has been largely improved with substantial reduction in number of main bursts from about 2 500 cases in 2000 by 98% to about 27 cases in 2024, and leakage rate from exceeding 25% in 2000 to about 13.4% in 2024. In order to maintain the healthiness of the water supply network, a risk-based water main asset management strategy is being implemented to maintain the healthiness of the water supply networks and reduce the risk of water main bursts or leaks. It is a proactive management strategy aimed to prevent as far as practicable the failure of the water mains by rendering priorities to those water mains with high risk for improvement works including replacement or rehabilitation. The risk is assessed taking into account various factors including the consequences of bursts or leaks, ages and materials of the water mains, past records of bursts or leaks, surrounding environment, etc. Besides, improvement works to water mains in “main burst hot spots” (i.e. locations with repeated water main bursts) are also carried out

Since 2016, the Water Supplies Department (WSD) has been establishing the Water Intelligence Network (WIN) and completed the setup of 2 400 District Metering Areas (DMAs) by the end of March 2025. The “Divide & Conquer” and “Continuous monitoring” strategies strengthen leakage management within the water supply network, maintaining the healthiness of the network.

Implementation of WIN enables problematic DMAs and PMAs to be prioritised for follow-up actions according to their degree of water loss with a view to maintaining the healthiness of the network. Progressive Adaptive Approach for Coastal Engineering

Considering the uncertainties in the range of possible future climate change development and global actions among nations on reducing carbon emissions, we adopt a progressive adaptive approach to formulate climate adaptation measures. We adequately plan and design our new coastal structure taking into account various greenhouse gas emissions scenarios including the very high scenario up to the end of 21st century, while we can allow provision (e.g. larger footing and buffer area) in advance and flexibly opt to enhance the infrastructure timely. This approach allows us to avoid excessive infrastructure development and premature hindrance to the public enjoyment of seafront during the current current timeframe. This progressive adaptive approach is designed to be flexible and adaptive enough so that the structure can be modified with reference to the latest development in climate change.

Adaptation, Resilience and Management for Shoreline Management 

For all coastal areas in Hong Kong, we continue to adopt a risk management approach to assess the likelihood and consequences of seawater inundation, with integrated
strategies of Adaptation, Resilience and Management to cope with the potentially increasing flood risks under the impacts of climate change. We identified 11 coastal areas planned for advance preparation to cope with the coastal risks near the mid-century. In collaboration with relevant departments and stakeholders, we will plan improvement measures involving public spaces and private properties through the “Hold The Line” strategy. The improvement measures will continue to adopt a multi-layered protection design to mitigate coastal flood risks and reduce the impacts of flooding. The multi-layered protection design includes:-

	Adopting adaptation measures along the coastline as the first line of defence to reduce the coastal hazards, for example, constructing or raising wave walls;
	Adopting resilience measures in suitable locations behind the coastline to form the second line of defence, for example, demountable flood barriers to form a buffer zone to further reduce the seawater flowing towards inland areas;
	Adopting contingency measures in front of important buildings as the third line of defence, for example, demountable flood boards and/or sandbags; and 
	Finally, in conjunction with management measures, such as early warning systems and action plans on emergency arrangement, installation of water gauges, pumps and warning signs, etc. to raise public alertness and strengthen preparedness.

Furthermore, we will proactively share the potential improvement options with relevant stakeholders and plan improvement measures in a timely manner to mitigate coastal flood risks at mid-century and strengthen the defence capability of the shoreline.

column16: Con el fin de considerar los retos y las posibles oportunidades de la acción climática como un mecanismo de justicia social, el análisis de la vulnerabilidad climática considera los datos del índice de vulnerabilidad social para identificar las características de la población susceptible de sufrir un daño, ya sea en su persona o en sus bienes, así como de conocer la capacidad de prevención, respuesta y organización frente a un evento climático. Los datos indican que el 11.4% de la población se encuentra en un nivel de vulnerabilidad social muy alto, el 21.8% está en un nivel de vulnerabilidad social alto, el 27.8% se encuentra en un nivel medio, el 23.4% está en un nivel bajo, y el 15.6% tiene una vulnerabilidad social muy baja. Desde la gestión integral de riesgos y la adaptación al cambio climático, esta información es relevante para identificar las prioridades de intervención para reducir riesgos, prevenir desastres asociados al cambio climático y fortalecer las capacidades de prevención, organización y respuesta de la población. En ese marco, existe una vulnerabilidad dual, donde la población tiene predisposición de ser afectados por el cambio climático y también por situaciones sociales que incrementan estos riesgos, como la discriminación, la inequidad y las necesidades básicas insatisfechas.

column16: En el ámbito hidráulico, la resiliencia requiere del conocimiento pleno de la infraestructura y de las reglas de operación que respondan tanto a condiciones normales como a situaciones de emergencia. Además, para ser resilientes, es necesario alcanzar el más alto nivel de eficacia en el manejo de recursos naturales disponible, asegurar la equidad en el acceso a éstos y garantizar la seguridad hídrica de los habitantes.Por otro lado , es necesario continuar con el uso sustentables del acuífero y contribuir a la planeación de la seguridad hídrica, lo que implica incorporar nuevas fuentes de abastecimiento, como el agua tratada, para satisfacer los usos de riego agrícola, industrial e incluso doméstico, en aquellas actividades que no requieren agua potable. Otra alternativa es la cosecha de agua de lluvia, que ha mostrado ventajas al aplicarse como una acción doméstica que satisface muchos usos en el hogar, por ello la importancia del programa \'Cosecha de agua de lluvia\' que desde 2019 ha beneficiado a habitantes de la Ciudad de México con la instalación de un sistema de captación de agua pluvial. Del 2019 a 2024 se han invertido casi 1 millón 418 mil de pesos para la instalación de más de 70 mil Sistemas de Captación de Agua de Lluvia en 11 Alcaldías (Azcapotzalco, Coyoacán, Gustavo A. Madero, Iztacalco, Iztapalapa, Magdalena Contreras, Milpa Alta, Tláhuac, Tlalpan, Venustiano Carranza y Xochimilco) de la Ciudad de México. Asimismo, desde 2023 con el proyecto Escuelas de Captación se han instalado más de 2,000 sistemas de captación de agua de lluvia (SCALL) en más de 1,800 planteles y espacios educativos de todos los niveles educativos en la Ciudad, con lo que se benefició a más de 1.3 millones de usuarios totales considerando personal y estudiantes

column16: Impacta directamente la adaptación al cambio climático (CC) porque reduce la capacidad de las ciudades y comunidades para enfrentar fenómenos extremos y mantener la resiliencia ambiental y social, debido a que los ecosistemas urbanos y periurbanos, como parques, bosques, humedales y áreas verdes, ayudan a regular la temperatura, la humedad y la calidad del aire. La pérdida de estos espacios aumenta el efecto de isla de calor urbano, empeorando olas de calor y reduciendo la capacidad de adaptación de la población; de igual forma los espacios verdes y ecosistemas absorben agua de lluvia y estabilizan el suelo por lo que su degradación genera mayor riesgo de inundaciones, deslizamientos y erosión, afectando infraestructura, viviendas y vidas humanas.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: El acceso al cuidado de la salud permite a las poblaciones enfrentar, resistir y recuperarse de los impactos asociados a fenómenos climáticos extremos, cambios en la distribución de enfermedades y condiciones ambientales adversas, ya que el cambio climático altera la frecuencia e intensidad de eventos como olas de calor, inundaciones o sequías, que a su vez pueden incrementar enfermedades respiratorias, gastrointestinales, cardiovasculares y transmitidas por vectores (dengue, chikungunya, zika), por ello el acceso a servicios de salud permite la prevención, diagnóstico temprano y tratamiento, disminuyendo la vulnerabilidad de la población frente a estos riesgos. El acceso a servicios de salud reduce la vulnerabilidad, mejora la resiliencia y permite una adaptación más efectiva a los efectos del cambio climático, especialmente para las poblaciones más expuestas o en situación de riesgo.

column14: Access to mobility and transport services (e.g. walk paths, cycle infrastructure, roads, public transport)
column16: El acceso a servicios de transporte y movilidad contribuye a la adaptación al cambio climático (CC) porque mejora la capacidad de las personas y comunidades para enfrentar, responder y recuperarse de los impactos climáticos, a la vez que puede disminuir riesgos y vulnerabilidades, por ejemplo, el acceso a bicisendas, transporte público eficiente y seguro disminuye la dependencia de vehículos privados, reduciendo emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero y contribuyendo indirectamente a mitigar los efectos del CC; los caminos y ciclovías diseñadas para condiciones climáticas extremas garantizan movilidad incluso durante eventos como lluvias intensas o calor extremo. En resumen, un sistema de transporte accesible, seguro y planificado climáticamente fortalece la capacidad de las personas y comunidades para adaptarse al cambio climático al garantizar movilidad segura, respuesta rápida ante emergencias y continuidad de servicios esenciales.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Cuando los ecosistemas y el entorno natural funcionan como “infraestructura verde” que ayuda a las personas y comunidades a enfrentar los impactos climáticos. Los ecosistemas como bosques, humedales y áreas verdes urbanas regulan la temperatura, reducen el efecto de islas de calor y modulan la humedad, esto ayuda a las personas a adaptarse a olas de calor, sequías o variaciones extremas de temperatura. Las condiciones ambientales favorables —ecosistemas intactos, espacios verdes funcionales, agua limpia y aire saludable— incrementan la capacidad de adaptación al cambio climático, reduciendo vulnerabilidades, protegiendo recursos y mejorando la resiliencia de las personas y comunidades.

Public education in Italy is provided free of charge, and schools represent the most common type of building used for public services. Data on the education system indicate a rise in educational attainment. Notably, the percentage of individuals aged 25 to 64 who have completed upper secondary education increased by 8% from 2012 (73.7%) to 2023 (81.9%).

Similarly, the proportion of people aged 30 to 34 who hold a university degree rose significantly, almost 20%, from 2012 (42.5%) to 2023 (62.4%).

These schoolyards are increasingly converted into cool green spaces during the summer months, serving as venues for community activities.

Therefore it wouldn't be completely correct to affirm that poverty is decreasing, but that the actual real estate market is pushing it away: the new Master Plan is already tackling this issue throw social housing policies and incentives, but the effect has not been observed yet.Poverty is one of the main challenges to improve climate adaptivity, both in the cold and the hot seasons: in winter the main issue is to ensure that nobody is going to be harmed by the low temperatures, reason why every year the Municipality of Milan issues the Plan Against Cold, as a support for homeless people; in summer, even though the hazard is less harmful, more people are exposed to high temperatures, since air conditioning systems are less diffused and more expensive than heating systems, furthermore there are not any plans to support who does not have access to an house.

column16: Regarding climate change related issues, Milan has high water availability, which lowers the risk of drought (meant as general lack of water): the large availability of this resource is a problem when the city has to face high amounts of water in a brief time, because this limits the capacity of the soil to stock it, so it increases the flood risk. Adaptive capacity is influenced as well by the capacity of a territory to be self sufficient in terms of electrical energy production and consumption: according to the Regional Plan for Energy and Environment (source: SIRENA20 - 2022 data), Lombardy is able to meet about 60% of its energy consumption autonomously. Of the electricity generated, 33% comes from renewable sources.

column16: According to the Consumer Price Index (source: Sistema Statistico Integrato - Comune di Milano), the cost of living seems to have significantly increased between 2016 and 2025, especially for basic goods like food and housing. This of course is a problem for the adaptive capacity of the city since citizens start having less resources: one of the main issues is the cost of housing, which in the last ten years increased drastically, making it harder for people to be able to afford a house in the city.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: As explained in the cost of living section, this is one of the main problems in Milan, in fact the price of housing has been increasing drastically in the past years and this is causing a mass gentrification, pushing the population towards the suburbs or other satellite cities, increasing the daily displacements and therefore raising the transport demand, in fact, between 2003 and 2013 Milan's public transport supply increased by 10.3% (source: PUMS). One of the main challenges for climate change adaptation policies, in relation with the housing issue, will be to plan green areas avoiding the gentrifying effect of the increased property value, which, according to many hedonic pricing studies, is associated with the availability of green areas. One of the main solutions that Milan is planning, is the estabilishment of bonuses for who provides a new building with social housing dedicated spaces.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The basic services in urban areas can be categorized in 1)Water distribution service 2)Drainage and sanitation 3)Energy distribution service and 4)Transport.The water distribution system is very efficient, as the loss of water from the network amounts to 11% of the total in Milan, while in Italy it reaches 39%. The network is very widespread: not only have houses access to potable water, but around the city there are also 565 drinking fountains used to prevent water stagnation in blind spots, which could lead to a water borne disease. Additionally, the Municipality and MM SpA installed the so called \'Case dell'acqua\' (Water houses), which provide package-free fresh water in 22 spots in the city. The sewage system is very efficient as well: since it was designed to host high amounts of water and to be very interconnected, it is able to redistribute water minimizing the flood risk. Regarding the sewage depuration system, Milan has three waste water treatment plants (WWTP): Milano San Rocco, Milano Nosedo and Peschiera Borromeo. Nosedo is the biggest plant in the city (its treatment capacity exceeds one million of equivalent inhabitants, 50% of the overall amount of sewage) and its efficiency allows the WWTP to be used for irrigation in the agricultural fields. The energy distribution network had issues during a heat wave in 2015 and 2021 summer, when the energy consumption increased rapidly and the system collapsed. It's important to underline the fact that the excessive energy demand was not the only cause of the blackout, but it was made worse by a particular type of electrical joints (self-shrink joints 24V) and the morphology of the network. At the end of the same year, the Energy Networks and Environment Regulation Authority (ARERA) released a regulation for energy distribution services, which the energy utility of Milan (Unareti) transposed developing the Intervention Plan for the Increase of the Network Resilience, which aims to avoid any kind of climate related issue (floods, strong winds and frost). In terms of physical accessibility, the public transport offer is commensurate with the density of the population, leaving the suburbs with fewer services. Milan remains the city with the highest local public transport offering in Italy, with 16,310 seat-kilometers per inhabitant. From a socio-economic point of view, the ATM (Milan Transport Agency) gives the citizens with a lower income the possibility to access the service at a subsidized cost.

Community engagement is crucial in public space renovation, particularly through initiatives like Piazze Aperte (Open Squares), which enhance social interaction via tactical urbanism. These low-budget, temporary interventions prioritize user experience and follow community engagement processes to understand local needs. This approach aims to create permanent, livable spaces that offer social benefits as well as urban cooling and sustainable drainage.

Another example of community engagement is the consultation during the drafting of the Air and Climate Plan, which included workshops and roundtables for citizen feedback. Additionally, the 'Adopt a Green Area' initiative encourages citizens to help maintain green spaces in Milan, while 'Shared Gardens' allows volunteers to manage degraded areas for community benefit. Public and private entities can also seek municipal support for projects aimed at regenerating urban spaces.
In 2024, as part of the GTNRC programme, the city conducted and published the first Community resilience assessment at the neighbourhood scale. The assessment's goal is to evaluate the resilience of the Crescenzago Neighbourhood to heat waves.The study represented the starting point for the co-design of soft measures to improve the resilience of the neighbourhood. column16: Participation and transparency are two of the main principles that guide Milan's governance: in fact, city plans are subject to public consultation and data has to be publicly available. But public engagement is not only assured by transparency policies and public consultations, but by other measures as well: the RCM Foundation developed an online platform, PartecipaMi, which allows the citizens to report certain issues in services, discuss or establish a dialogue with the public administration. Another example is the presence of the municipality on social networks, reporting news and problems in Milan and giving to the citizens the chance to express their concerns and opinions.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Italy in general provides its citizens with free healthcare. Regarding the quality of Milan healthcare, data (source: Sistema Statistico Integrato - Comune di Milano) suggests that between 2000 and 2022 the total amount of days spent in hospital decreased by more than 40%, while the population increased by 4,51% and the number of hospital admissions decreased by over 35%: this suggests that the healthcare system could have become not only more efficient and effective, but that the citizens probably started living healtier lives.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Data suggests that in the last years crime rates generally peaked between 2010 and 2014 and decreased again, the only crime typology that constantly increased since 2004 is cyber-crime (eg phishing). In the national classification, Milan has the highest crime rates (source: Il Sole 24 Ore): it's important to underline the fact that this data has been calculated on the base of registered complaints to the police, which means that of course there is criminality, but that people are not afraid to file a complaint as well. All these facts suggest that Milan suffers from the stress of micro criminality, but what really could affect the city are cyber-attacks, that in the last years have been used as a weapon to take cities as hostages, disabling their systems and blocking the decisional processes that are essential to guarantee the functioning of a city, especially if the city has to face climate change related shocks. Another indicator that could be taken into account is the amount of transport related accidents, in particular the amount of injured in road accidents fell by more than 50% between 2001 and 2024. this suggests that the safety in Milan's streets is imrpving, which is fundamental to encourage bicycle use.
