column16:
Data suggests that unemployment rate in Milan has one of the lowest values in Italy, therefore, even though it still has to be tackled, is not considered a major issue. 
In 2024, the number of jobs in Milan increased by 28,000 unit, representing a 1.9% rise above the national average. Approximately half of these new positions were filled by women. With an additional 13,000 female workers compared to 2023, the total number of women in the workforce in Milan surpassed 700,000 for the first time. Women now make up 45.9% of the overall workforce.

This growth in the Milan labor market is solely attributed to the service sector, while the industrial sector is experiencing a decline.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Migration can be considered from two points of view: immigration and emigration. Immigration, which in Milan more than doubled since 1999, in Italy as in many nations in the rest of Europe has been a major issue, mainly because of the needs of regularizing the new citizens and of providing more services for many more people with a low income. The other issue that Italy is facing is the emigration of young people with a university degree: data shows that, even though the overall amount of residents in Milan increased by almost 60000 of people in the last 20 years, the amount of local residents decreased by almost 111000 of people. This means that Milan as Italy is losing potentially medium-high income citizens and gaining low-income ones, which in the long term will be likely to cause the city and the whole nation to lose wealth.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: According to data reported by the Italian Institute of Statistics In 2022, Milan had the highest GDP per capita in the province, reaching €66,600, which is nearly double the national average of €33,800. \n\nThe most profitable sectors in Milan include finance, real estate, and professional services, contributing €22,700 per capita. Following these are commerce, public services, transportation, and telecommunications, which together contribute €18,600 per capita

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Milan's economy development and high land value made the city very attractive for real estate and building business: in this case the only way prevent the city from losing too much permeable soil is a strict regulation, which is a matter of land use planning. Milan's new Masterplan (PGT) aims to the improvement of environmental quality and the protection of permeable soil through new standards, as the article 10 of the document, which enforces a more resilient approach to buildings regulation, decreasing the energy requirement and increasing the amount of permeable spaces like green roofs and walls. In addition, for the first time Milan takes on the production of ecosystem services as a form of natural resource useful to support greenhouse gas and carbon emissions reduction and to mitigate extreme events (heat islands, peaks in air pollution, torrential rains). To meet the challenges posed by urbanization, the PGT sets itself these objectives related to greenery and land consumption:- reduction of land consumption rate, with the identification of 1.7 million m2 of non-building areas and protection of 3.5 million m2 of new agricultural areas;- safeguarding future green areas;- creation of 20 new parks within the city;- planning of a large Metropolitan Park around Milan, which connects the new parks to the existing ones;- identification of an ecological network, with areas of depavimentation, planting and reforestation contributing to the ForestaMI project that aims to plant 3 million trees in the metropolitan city.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Social inequality is usually described by the Gini coefficient, a number between 0 -perfect equality- and 1 -total inequality- which in Milan, in the past 10 years (2008-2017) oscillated around 0.53 (source: calculated on the household income data from Sistema Statistico Integrato - Comune di Milano): therefore, in Milan, income inequality it's worse than the national average (around 0.31) and, in general, it's higher than the rest of the European countries (around 0.30). Inequality causes challenges for climate change adaptation that are similar to the ones caused by poverty, with the further problem that income differences, which cause wealth and poverty, are not directly geographically traceable for a matter of privacy, therefore it is harder to implement solutions that consider this issue.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The most relevant economic sector in Milan is commerce, intended as both wholesale, retail and vehicles reparation. The second and third sectors are professional, scientific and technical activities, followed by the manufacturing sector. Furthermore, Milan is the second agricultural capital in Italy, counting a 16% of farmed land. This data suggests that Milan is rich in terms of economic diversity, covering all the economic sectors.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The City of Milan recognise the Open Government as the paradigm to create an open Public Administration that support innovation within citizens and businesses, and open data is one of the cornerstones of this strategy. The fundamental principle of open data is that public data, in compliance with current legislation, belong to the community and as such must be re-usable by anyone who has an interest in it. Since not everybody is able to read data, the municipality of Milan made several informative systems available and it's still working to improve data accessibility. As a result, Milan Municipality created an open data portal: https://dati.comune.milano.it/. This particular service is very useful for climate change adaptation policies because gives to private businesses, organizations/associations and universities the chance to participate and be informed about certain issues. There are countless datasets publicly available that describe climate, population, built environment, economy, services, health and more.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Data shows that life expectancy increased in the last 20 years and post-partum mortality rates decreased by almost 50%. In these years the main health related issue in Milan is a low air quality, which does not only physically affect people, but it generates a constant psychological stress on the citizens: the relationship between low air quality and adaptivity is direct, in fact people with respiratory and cardiovascular issues, as well as overweight people, are more sensitive to the effect of extreme temperatures. Following the pandemic event, the Health Protection Agency of the metropolitan city of Milan quantify a 50% mortality rate increase observed in the first quarter of 2020 when compared to the expected mortality of the previous four years (2016-2019).

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Many buildings are not adapted to climate hazards such as floods or heatwaves, and this is even more challenging for vulnerable population. In Paris, 22.5% of households with two or more people live in housing that is too small for the size of their household (APUR, 2020). Post-war buildings, up until the turn of the 2000s, paid very little attention to the summer habitability of buildings. The negative effects of heatwaves, especially felt inside homes, are even more acute when public spaces have limited vegetation and when asphalt absorbs heat (urban heat island effect).

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The cost of living in Paris is very high. This can lead to difficulties in finding accommodation, renovating housing, accessing healthcare, avoiding nuisances, consuming organic and local foods, etc. The inability to improve the summer habitability for certain households leads to an increase in morbidity/mortality among the most vulnerable individuals (elderly, sick, or isolated).

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Some transport infrastructures are highly challenged. Built environment and public spaces:When public spaces are poorly vegetated and buildings have been constructed without considering summer habitability, the negative effects of heatwaves are more acute.A flood represents a major risk to the very structure of buildings. Certain sites could trigger domino effects: hospitals, city hall, transportation hubs, soil destabilization, network disruptions, and material damage.Transportation and mobility:A heatwave makes walking and cycling difficult.A major flood of the Seine would cause enormous material risks: entry of mud and debris into tunnels, destruction of tracks, malfunctions of electrical equipment. An unmanaged flood would have an impact on all lines and paralyze the entire transport network.Storms can cause localized damages (falling of a relay antenna).Communication network:Heatwaves pose the main threat to telecommunications: antennas, highly exposed to the sun and typically located on rooftops, have power supplies with electronics sensitive to high temperatures. Heat also leads to overheating of data centers, which require cooling.Public health system:The healthcare provision in Paris is exposed to numerous hazards. Each facility needs a continuous supply of potable water, electricity, heating, and cooling, making the healthcare system particularly sensitive to climate hazards and domino effects.A power outage, a flood, or a scarcity of water resources (each hospital bed consumes an average of 750 liters of water daily) can result in partial interruptions of healthcare services. This can lead to growing needs of the population. Cold waves, and even more so, heatwaves, can lead to spikes in hospitalizations and mortality, particularly among vulnerable individuals: the elderly, young children, and people experiencing homelessness.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Budgets are not necessarily directed towards climate objectives. However, steps are taken to assess the share of the budget meeting the mitigation and adaptation objectives (green budgeting). Paris is undertaking the process of adopting the methodology for evaluating expenditure from the perspective of climate change adaptation (I4CE methodology).\n\nAdditionally, Paris is developing its Climate Budgeting, in order to better quantify the financial needs, as well as the provided investments, associated to its mitigation and adaptation targets. Thus far in 2025, the City tracks up to 890 M€ for 2024 (more than half of its entire investment budget) as investments as contributing to its climate action plan. First estimations regarding local mitigation (buildings and transport) assess a need of an additional 400 M€ of yearly investments, mainly linked to subsidies to private renovations and the global renovation of city buildings. Further estimations are aimed at better quantifying adaptation and footprint needs.

column16: Today, there are major challenges in terms of regulation. Indeed, regulatory documents such as the local urban plan are not necessarily adapted to the objectives of the Climate Plan, but could be extremely effective levers to meet these objectives. Work is currently underway to further orient these documents in favor of mitigation and adaptation.Despite the creation of 80 hectares of new parks and gardens since 2006, Paris remains a predominantly urban city (with 84% of its soils being impermeable, excluding forests).

column16: Political engagement in Paris enables the administration to work on these issues. The Mayor of Paris was president of C40 from 2016 to 2019. Paris elaborated its first climate plan on a volountary basis in 2007.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: On one hand, the environment has become a major factor in migration and displacement around the world. In 2015, three times as many people displaced by natural disasters only because of wars and violence. So a World Bank report of March 2018 evokes 143 million climate migrants from hereto 2050. Currently, while the city is hosting more and more migrants, living conditions of migrants are not satisfying in Paris. On the other hand, the COVID 19 crisis shows also that crisis may reduce Paris' attractiveness.In order to enhance knowledge on climate migrations and their consequences for the Parisian territory, the City signed a Research Convention with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in 2021.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: In Paris, community engagement can foster new lifestyles and boost solidarity (Paris volunteers).Since 2001, citizen participation has been a major focus of the municipal policy in Paris.In order to support the most vulnerable Parisians during extreme summer heat, Paris has implemented the assistance and support program called \'REFLEX.\' Elderly, sick, or isolated individuals can register for this program. In the event of a Heatwave Plan activation, registered individuals are contacted by phone to check on their health status and provide assistance if necessary.Currently, more than 10,000 people are registered in the REFLEX database and receive personalized assistance during periods of high heat. In 2022, all registered individuals were called, and 158 home visits were organized.The city of Paris has created a \'Summer Solidarity Guide 2023\' to address the challenges faced by individuals in extreme precarious situations or without a fixed abode during the summer. Various support measures are listed on the website: https://www.paris.fr/pages/le-guide-solidarite-a-paris-ete-2023-est-disponible-23880During the summer of 2023, the \'Night of Solidarity\' will take place, which involves outreach activities targeting individuals experiencing homelessness. Water bottles provided by Eau de Paris will be distributed.In 2022, \'Climate Volunteers\' were mobilized to improve the urban cooling island map of Paris. Additionally, the city conducted climate walks focusing on urban cooling themes.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The city of Paris benefits from high quality expertise and data. Administration and agencies are working more and more on mitigation and adaptation issues. More and more data, apps, are available for the public. Paris made data available through its opendata platform.The cooling island map is available in open data. This map identifies and lists various naturally cool or refreshed places accessible to the public during hot weather. Currently, there are over 1300 cooling islands available during the day (drinking fountains, misters, shaded areas, public showers, outdoor swimming areas, air-conditioned libraries, Oasis school playgrounds, parks, and gardens).During days of intense heat, citizens can get real-time information on pollution and air quality index in Paris through AirParif.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Land use planning can enable to transform public spaces, a greater place for water and nature, build a sustainable city.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Some public services are not adapted to the high density of population of the city. The need for sustainable collective cooling solutions for Parisian buildings, as well as the limitation and reduction of environmental impacts associated with air conditioning, represents a major challenge in the perspective of a resilient and carbon-neutral city by 2050. In order to address this issue and improve the summer habitability of buildings, Paris is developing its urban heating and cooling networks. In April 2022, Paris entrusted the development of this public service to \'Fraîcheur de Paris.\' Currently, more than 700 buildings are connected to the Parisian urban cooling network (93 kilometers of networks). The objective is to triple the size of this network by 2042 (252 kilometers).

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Education and schools more and more take into account climate and adaptation issues.The city of Paris created the Climate Academy in 2021. In partnership with this organization, the educational program called \'Adapting to Climate Change in the City\' was launched in September 2021. This academic course is intended for students aged 9 to 15.For the general public, in 2021, a MOOC (Massive Open Online Course) on \'Adapting to Climate Change\' was created in partnership with ADEME (French Environment and Energy Management Agency) and the Observatory for Sustainable Real Estate (OID).Starting from 2023, Paris plans to offer its employees a training program on the Climate Plan, particularly focusing on climate change adaptation. The objective is to familiarize all city employees with the topic of climate change.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The City of Paris has set up public health policies and systems in many areas (healthcare provision, prevention, health promotion, environmental health, etc.) supported by central services (prevention and screening office, school health office, access to healthcare office, environmental health service, health promotion and inequality reduction unit, mental health and resilience unit, etc.) and local structures (health centers, medico-social centers, prevention structures, etc.). They are also relayed by territorial entities (territorial health teams, city health workshops, etc.). Public policy on resilience, mitigation and adaptation to climate change and environmental health, which aims to identify risks, prevent them or reduce their effects on health.Development of a health observatory, taking into account population vulnerabilities and environmental health.Moreover, in addition to liberal and hospital medicine and the presence of university research teams, there are a large number of health centers in Paris, both municipal and private. The assistance to the installation of private practicing structures grouped in sector 1, constitutes a strong axis of the municipality. These structures are able to meet the challenges of the fight against social inequalities in health and the development of prevention. Since 2016, the city has created the Paris Environmental Health Plan.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The city of Paris conducted a crisis management exercise in 2016 (SEQUANA) to assess its capacity to handle a major flood. For October 2023, Paris is preparing the \'Paris at 50°C\' exercise to better respond to an extreme heat scenario. This crisis exercise will be based on an unprecedented heatwave scenario (heat dome at 50°C) and will involve local residents and municipal establishments such as schools, daycare centers, nursing homes, etc.Heatwave Plan: To limit the consequences of extreme temperature episodes, the City of Paris has implemented various prevention and communication measures:- It maintains meteorological monitoring to anticipate heatwaves.- It has established the REFLEX program, allowing vulnerable Parisians to be monitored and supported during periods of extreme heat.- Regular phone calls are made to check on their situation.- It sets up a network of \'cooled\' rooms throughout the capital.- It implements measures and actions to raise awareness and protect the population from the health consequences of a heatwave.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Presence of major hospital facilities, including specialized services for tropical infectious diseases.Density of doctors per capita higher than the national average (but a significant part of the supply is not financially accessible to all).Large number of health centers providing access to care at the agreed rate.Significant financial and spatial inequalities in access to healthcare: proportion of general practitioners with a particular mode of practice (authorizing fees above the social security ceiling) much higher than the national average, low proportion of specialists in sector 1, non-homogeneous distribution of doctors across the country.Decrease in the number of doctors in the country and accelerated ageing of the medical profession in recent years.Training of health professionals to be adapted in the future for the detection of diseases still little or not present on the territory.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: WATER: The phenomenon of aggravated droughts in the medium and long terms poses the problem of the water supply of Paris and its region, both for drinking water needs and for agricultural and industrial uses. This problem must consider the scale of the Seine basin.ENERGY: Paris is very dependent on external energy supplies. Local energy production and consumption control will become essential to maintain the local economy (including tourism), the living conditions of households, the quality of transport... This issue can only be addressed through a long-term metropolitan approach and by integrating the context global energy.BIODIVERSITY: Biodiversity can be considered both vulnerable to climate change (droughts, heat waves, floods,migration of species ...) and as a response to adapt to the new conditions (planting to fight the heat by city, to limit the effects of heavy rains, diversify to better resist changes, etc.). This issue is apprehended in the short and medium term, at the building, district, city and metropolitan scales.FOOD: Due to the various fragilities and pressures weighing on the regional agricultural development model (current lack diversification of crops, increased urbanization, etc.) and increased dependence on irrigation, productions may be more sensitive to events extreme climates (droughts in particular). Indeed, if the irrigation water needs are not met, this will necessarily have consequences for the city's supply (rising prices, tensions on the agricultural markets, even ruptures supply).AIR: In Paris, a significant portion (72%) of PM2.5 emissions from road traffic is attributed to brake, tire, and road abrasion. Heatwaves can lead to ozone peaks, and measures are taken if threshold exceedances persist. To enhance public awareness of air pollution risks, Paris is actively increasing its information sources and understanding of atmospheric pollutants. The city is involved in multiple initiatives and conducting specific studies:Pollutrack project, Exemplaair and also the ANR sTREEt project.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Social, health and environmental inequalities exist in Paris. They reduce the capacity of adaptation of the population. A study has shown which neighbourhoods cumulate such inequalities. Policies should be targetted to reduce these inequalities by creating new public services .These social inequalities have taken a different form: Precarity no longer affects only isolated and homeless individuals; it now affects families, low-wage workers, and migrants who face additional barriers to integration. This precariousness has significant impacts in terms of inadequate housing (energy poverty, substandard living conditions) and difficulties in accessing housing (nearly 2,200 families were deprived of housing in Paris in 2016).Furthermore, nature is unevenly distributed across the Parisian territory. To reduce this inequality, Paris aims to increase accessibility to nature through the creation of green spaces, the reduction of impermeable surfaces, and the greening of buildings

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The City of Paris has established public health policies and systems in various domains, such as healthcare provision, prevention, health promotion, environmental health, and more. These efforts are backed by central services like the prevention and screening office, school health office, access to healthcare office, environmental health service, health promotion and inequality reduction unit, mental health and resilience unit, among others. Local structures, including health centers, medico-social centers, and prevention structures, also play a vital role in implementing these policies. Additionally, territorial entities, such as territorial health teams and city health workshops, help in disseminating and reinforcing the public health initiatives.There is also a public policy concerning resilience, mitigation, and adaptation to climate change and environmental health, with the objective of identifying risks, preventing them, or mitigating their impact on health. A health observatory has been developed, considering the vulnerabilities of the population and environmental health aspects. Since 2016, the city has initiated the Paris Health and Environment Plan.

This map identifies and lists different naturally cool or refreshing places accessible to users when it's hot. Currently, there are over 1,300 cool islands accessible during the day, including drinking fountains, misting devices, shade structures, public showers, outdoor swimming areas, air-conditioned libraries, Oasis schoolyards, parks, and gardens.During days of high heat, citizens can stay informed in real time about pollution and air quality index in Paris through AirParif.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Built Environment and Public Spaces:To adapt to future heatwaves, Paris focuses on de-paving, greening, and tree planting. Currently, there are 80 vegetated streets and 40 \'School Streets.\' By 2026, the goal is to create 180 School Streets in 230 schools, de-pave 100 hectares, and plant 170,000 trees. Over 25,000 trees, including 800 on streets, were planted between November 2022 and April 2023. From 2018 to 2022, 100 schoolyards became \'Oasis Yards,\' with 14,000 square meters of green space and 121 trees. column16: The majority (nearly 70%) of Philadelphia's energy use comes from buildings, but a building and housing stock analysis completed in 2022 showed that 93% of the total buildings in the city are residential. Of these residential buildings, 91% are single-family homes, and 65% are 80-100 years old. While it is clear that the condition of Philadelphia's housing stock contributes to city-wide emissions and high rates of energy burden (particularly amongst low-income residents), the scope for residential decarbonization and adaptation is large and will require significant support and investment. In addition, Philadelphia is currently facing a housing crisis. According to the Department of Planning and Development and the American Community Survey, over 4,000 people are experiencing homelessness in Philadelphia, and 40% of the city's households are cost burdened. As such, housing has become a top priority of the current mayoral administration. \nThe Office of Sustainability is working ensure that the issues surrounding housing, energy, and climate change are interwoven and that the transition to clean energy is equitable and just.

This perception makes it hard to prioritize funding these efforts over issues that are perceived to be here and now. An estimated 12 percent of San Francisco residents were in poverty in 2023, and vulnerable groups such as older residents, women, and minority communities are more likely to be in poverty. column16:
San Francisco is in a housing affordability crisis with housing costs that have increased far faster than inflation since the late 1990s; housing became acutely expensive during the economic boom after 2011. With the lack of affordable housing, insufficient overall housing production, and an influx of higher income households, the city has seen an increase in cost burdens and a drop in low- and moderate-income households, certain racial/ethnic groups, and household types. Simultaneously, San Francisco has a long-standing commitment to invest in housing affordable at low and moderate incomes and to protect tenants with local ordinances on rent control and just cause eviction. Despite these efforts, the city has struggled to substantially improve housing affordability for low and moderate-income households. Between 1990 and 2015, the total number of severely rent burdened households (who spend over 30% of income on housing) in San Francisco increased from roughly 38,000 to 49,000. According to the San Francisco Examiner, in 2023 approximately 39% of San Francisco households paid more than 30% of their paycheck to rent and other housing costs. 

These housing issues impact the City's adaptive capacity in numerous ways. The lack of affordable housing has led workers to seek housing in less expensive areas outside of the City, which can increase GHG emissions related to commuting (particularly for those who drive). San Francisco's housing stock is also largely comprised of older buildings, which complicates and increases the cost of electrification and other upgrades that can help with mitigating climate change and improving climate adaptation. The housing crisis also detracts from the city's ability to address climate change because limited financial resources have to be split across competing issues.

San Francisco's General Obligation (GO) bond rating acts as the City's credit rating and is a measure of the overall financial stability of the City. In order to fund large capital projects, the City issues bonds, or debt, and the purchase of those bonds provides the financing for these capital projects. The city's high credit ratings allow the local government to issue debt at lower borrowing costs, while presenting minimal credit risk. However, the city currently faces a budget deficit, which has resulted in budget reductions across the board for almost all city departments, and has impacted funding availability for climate mitigation and adaptation projects. 
Additionally, the current federal administration's ending of climate funding has had a significant impact; San Francisco has had multiple major already-awarded grants rescinded.\

Os efeitos da mudança do clima atingem potencialmente os agricultores familiares, que frequentemente não possuem recursos para implementar medidas de adaptação. Esses agricultores, contudo, podem se beneficiar de políticas públicas incentivadoras para proteção de áreas prestadoras de serviços ambientais e da demanda por produtos agroecológicos. Esses pequenos produtores têm um papel crucial na promoção da adaptação do ecossistema local por meio de métodos de produção mais sustentáveis (Brasil/MMA, s.d.).Além desses impactos, relacionados diretamente com a produção de alimentos, a segurança alimentar nas cidades adquire outro componente importante quanto pensamos na logística para o armazenamento e distribuição dos alimentos. As ameaças ligadas às inundações e as ondas de calor podem afetar as infraestruturas como centros de distribuição e rotas de abastecimento devido a localização, como, por exemplo, proximidade de cursos d'água, custos com refrigeração e, inclusive, deterioração e perda de alimentos.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.

Estes têm baixa capacidade de manter a temperatura corporal em função ou da necessidade de formação do processo de termorregulação após o nascimento, ou da perda do termorregulador denominado gordura marrom. Estudo confirma que eventos de ondas de calor têm se tornado frequentes na cidade de São Paulo. Zonas amplamente povoadas por idosos e com vulnerabilidade alta, como se observa em alguns bairros das zonas Leste e Norte, apresentam maior risco. No Município de São Paulo, ocorrem diferenças de até 10 °C no gradiente horizontal de temperatura, com as mais altas temperaturas nas regiões centrais, mais urbanizadas, e as mais baixas nas periferias serranas ou próximas aos grandes reservatórios de água. As temperaturas elevadas podem, ainda, potencializar a probabilidade de ocorrência de dilatação de trilhos de trens, vazamentos, explosões, incêndios, rompimentos ou danos em coberturas, cabeamentos, torres de flare etc.

O primeiro decorre da própria condição climática, ou seja, variação de temperatura, pluviosidade, ventos etc., causando diretamente as condições de mortalidade ou morbidade. O segundo se dá de forma indireta, com o clima favorecendo o surgimento de doenças infecciosas, causadas por vetores, que geram consequências físicas, psicológicas, nutricionais etc.

column16: Warsaw's adaptive capacity revolves largely around the city's natural system and blue-green infrastructure system. The most characteristic natural element of Warsaw's landscape is the Vistula River valley, protected under the Natura 2000 European nature network. Warsaw is located in a temperate, moderate, transitional climate zone. During the year, continental and oceanic air masses flow over the city, resulting in a wide variety of weather conditions. At the same time, the capital is distinguished by a relatively large share of land with natural functions, which accounted for about 47% of its area at the end of December 2023. The city is surrounded by vast, naturally valuable areas of natural and semi-natural character. These include forests, meadows, wetlands and river valleys, as well as agricultural areas with fertile soils. Together they form the extensive Green Ring of Warsaw. It serves as a buffer for the expanding metropolitan agglomeration. It also serves as places of rest and recreation for residents. About 43% of these areas are the most environmentally valuable, subject to various forms of nature protection (including a national park, 74 reserves, 3 landscape parks, areas belonging to the Natura 2000 network). As much as 27% of the city's area is covered by legal forms of nature protection. Related areas of high natural value are also located within the administrative boundaries of the capital. The above conditions result in Warsaw being a city with high natural potential favourable for the formation of a system of blue-green infrastructure. The highest and high predisposition in this regard is shown by 39% of the areas, and moderate - 19%. The weak point here is the hydrographic network within the city limits which, as a result of strong and long-term urbanization processes, is significantly impoverished and requires restoration and renaturalization.

column16:
Gentrification affects Zurich's ability to adapt to climate change in several interconnected ways.

First, gentrification-driven displacement and rising housing costs can undermine community stability and social cohesion—key factors that enhance collective resilience to climate threats like floods, heatwaves, and storms. When low-income and vulnerable populations are displaced to suburban or less-resilient areas, their access to climate-adaptive infrastructure and services diminishes, increasing their risks and straining municipal adaptation efforts.

Second, social inequality exacerbated by gentrification can limit equitable participation in climate adaptation planning and resource allocation. Inclusive community engagement is crucial for tailoring effective local climate resilience strategies, but displacement and segregation fragment neighborhoods and weaken the social networks that foster cooperation and local knowledge-sharing.

Third, gentrification accelerates urban redevelopment and densification, which can present both opportunities and challenges for climate adaptation. New construction can incorporate green infrastructure, energy-efficient technologies, and improved flood defenses, boosting urban resilience if well planned. However, rapid redevelopment also risks prioritizing private profit over holistic climate planning, potentially neglecting vulnerable areas or creating barriers to affordable, adaptive housing.

Fourth, the scarcity of affordable housing caused by gentrification intensifies pressure on land use and urban planning. This limits options for implementing large-scale climate adaptation infrastructure like parks, wetlands, or heat-reduction projects in densely populated or economically pressured neighborhoods.

Overall, gentrification's social and spatial impacts complicate Zurich's climate adaptation by challenging the inclusion, equity, and resilience of urban communities while simultaneously shaping the physical urban environment. To bolster climate adaptation, Zurich's government must integrate housing, social policy, and climate resilience planning holistically to ensure that vulnerable populations are protected, sustainable redevelopment is promoted, and collaboration across stakeholders is strengthened.

This aligns with research emphasizing the necessity of community stability, inclusivity, and equitable resource access as foundational elements of effective climate resilience in urban jurisdictions.

column16: Fortaleza tem avançado de forma consistente no engajamento social e na transparência de suas ações climáticas, estruturando uma governança em múltiplos níveis. O Gabinete de Governança Climática consolidou-se como secretariado deliberativo voltado às mudanças climáticas; o Observatório Climático, lançado em 2025, passou a funcionar como infraestrutura de dados e transparência; o Comitê Climático, previsto na minuta da Política Municipal de Mudança do Clima, atuará como corpo técnico-executivo de acompanhamento das ações; e o FORCLIMA foi fortalecido como instância de participação social consultiva. Em 2025, já foram realizadas três edições do FORCLIMA, incluindo uma dedicada às contribuições para a minuta da Política Municipal de Mudança do Clima e outra voltada à priorização de propostas oriundas da 1ª Conferência Municipal de Meio Ambiente, da Conferência das Cidades e de fóruns territoriais, sistematizadas para subsidiar a atualização do Plano de Ação Climática. Observa-se, nesse processo, um aumento significativo da participação social, tanto em número de atores envolvidos quanto na diversidade de contribuições incorporadas às decisões.\n\nEsse arranjo evidencia que grande parte das articulações e apoios obtidos inicialmente se ancorava no compromisso da gestão em inscrever projetos em iniciativas de financiamento e suporte técnico, alinhar-se a metas climáticas internacionais e manter o reporte de forma transparente. Atualmente, tais avanços encontram respaldo crescente na estrutura legislativa e de governança da cidade. O fortalecimento da participação social, aliado à transparência dos dados, garante legitimidade ao processo decisório e amplia a capacidade de adaptação do município, acelerando a evolução de Fortaleza na agenda climática — desde a elaboração de instrumentos de planejamento até a implementação de projetos concretos que fortalecem a resiliência urbana.

column16: The City of Miami's budgetary capacity significantly supports its adaptive capacity through the Miami Forever Bond. This $400 million General Obligation Bond funds critical resilience projects, including flood prevention, sea-level rise mitigation, affordable housing, parks, cultural facilities, roadway improvements, and public safety initiatives. The Citywide Stormwater Master Plan, approved by the Miami Commission, identifies 25 priority flood prevention projects that will be funded through a combination of the Miami Forever Bond, grants, and the City's capital budget. This Bond funding gives the City the ability to provide fund-matching for grants so it can be leveraged for greater impact. As of January 2025, $272,892,474 total project funds have been issued from the Bond.

column16: The City has partnerships with local universities as well as national organizations to provide climate data. As a \'tip of the spear\' City, many organizations look to partner with us. The City has access to flood report data from residents, worked with NOAA to map urban heat islands, receives data from Google Environmental Insights Explorer, and recently had a consultant group digitize records of the City's stormwater system and develop a Citywide flood model. The City completed its Vulnerability Assessment in 2024, which identified critical assets that could be harmed by flooding. For the City of Miami's Building Efficiency Program (BE305), to assist with implementation, the City procured a technical assistance and software partner, Touchstone IQ, who assisted with tracking and reporting of data, outreach to building owners and managing a help desk with dedicated sustainability consultants. City of Miami partnered with the CAPA Strategies Heatwatch program to engage citizen scientists, collect ambient heat data, and generate a Citywide GIS heatmap. In 2025, the City launched a new participatory science project, “Heat Sensors in Homes,” which has residents in the City's climate justice communities host indoor and outdoor heat sensors at their homes for a three month period over the summer to provide the City with data on lived experience of residents and heat variability throughout the City. Criteria for participation included income, energy burden, and persons with risk factors to extreme heat including children, elderly, and immunocompromised.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The reason for significant challenges is that the City of Miami has experienced substantial increases in construction costs due to several factors. These include rising prices for building materials, labor shortages, and increased demand for construction services. The cost of key materials such as steel, concrete, and lumber has surged, driven by supply chain disruptions and heightened global demand. Labor costs have also escalated as the construction industry faces a shortage of skilled workers. These factors collectively contribute to higher project costs, necessitating increased budget allocations to ensure the successful completion of infrastructure projects. According to the City's Stormwater Master Plan, the City has roughly $3.5-5 billion in unfunded needs to address priority upgrades of the City's stormwater system. Despite grants and funding from the City's general obligation fund, there are still funding shortfalls to meet this funding need. However, increased grant funding in recent years has been very helpful. In addition, the City will likely have to pay a significant cost share as a beneficiary of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Back Bay project.

column16: For years, City of Miami has been characterized by a rapid rate of urban development. A significant amount of new residential and commercial capacity has come online in recent years, and the pace of development is projected to continue. Rapid urbanization and development increase the demands on existing infrastructure, putting pressure on the City to increase service capacity. Increasing residents and businesses require more water, waste services, and room to move and recreate. The rapid pace of development makes clear the importance of developing more sustainable and resilient building and construction practices. As densification occurs in lower-income neighborhoods, residents may face rising costs of living, reduced affordability, and potential displacement due to climate impacts (e.g., flooding). Increasing population also stresses transit as public transit is widespread and roads are already in heavy use during peak hours.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The City of Miami is known for its strong Emergency Management teams and response capabilities. Emergency Managers in the City understand the life-safety threats posed by climate change, including rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and increased flooding, and have embraced a climate-focused mission to address these evolving challenges. This proactive approach is an asset in cultivating buy-in from residents, city leaders, and stakeholders, while fostering essential interdepartmental collaboration. \nThe City enhances its adaptive capacity through initiatives such as the interdepartmental King Tide Action Group, which focuses on preparing for the impacts of seasonal high tides, the relaunch of the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) program to expand volunteer engagement, and the implementation of a heat alert text service through the Everbridge platform to provide real-time notifications on extreme heat events. These efforts streamline communication, enhance flood mitigation, and improve emergency responses. \nIn 2024, the City held five CERT basic training sessions, and two in 2025, with two additional CERT training sessions scheduled, training over 80 new volunteers who will play a vital role in community preparedness and response. The continued engagement of residents, especially those in vulnerable communities, is a priority in ensuring that every resident, regardless of income or location, has the resources and support needed in the face of disaster.

The City's Area Median Income (AMI) is lower than surrounding areas but as the urban core of the region, there is an influx of interest in living in the City leading to concerns of gentrification and displacement. Waterfront properties worry about their ability to withstand flooding and potential increases in flood insurance. Lower income neighborhoods that are inland and on high ground worry about displacement if high elevation areas begin to densify. Housing affordability and availability remains a major source of stress on Miami's residents. Housing prices have markedly increased in recent years, placing burden on Miami residents. Throughout the pandemic, Miami topped lists of the country's most expensive places to live; according to US News and World Report Miami is the 4th Most Expensive Place to Live in the US in 2023-2024. According to the real estate firm Redfin the City of Miami is the second most unaffordable city to live in the US according to 2024 data. According to 2023 ACS data, the homeownership rate in the City of Miami is 33.4%. This indicates a high level of renters that reside in the City. In Miami-Dade County, Black and Latino households are more likely to be cost-burdened. Nearly half (48%) of Black and Latino households fall into this category, compared to 38-41% of other households. Lower homeownership rates among Black and Latino households contribute to this disparity. Affordability is affecting not only the low-income sector but the middle income and workforce population. The lack of affordability for the low-income group results in the loss of interest in seeking employment in the area, which can decrease human capital.

column16: Grant funding has been a major asset in Miami's ability to adapt to climate change and invest in smart and resilient infrastructure. The Grants department helps secure grants and external funding for projects aimed at improving the city's resilience to climate change, sea level rise, and other environmental challenges. This includes funding for infrastructure improvements, green spaces, and renewable energy initiatives. The department provides technical support to ensure that all funded projects comply with federal, state, and local regulations. Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) grants have given the City the ability to raise seawalls for projects that provide waterfront access to the public. State of Florida Resilient Florida funding has given the City the ability to invest in stormwater infrastructure improvements Citywide. Additionally, the City of Miami has the Miami Forever Bond, a $400 million initiative aimed at enhancing the City's resilience through flood prevention, infrastructure improvements, and green space development. It also supports public safety and affordable housing projects to ensure a sustainable and resilient future for all residents.

column16: Low-to-Moderate Income (LMI) populations in Miami face significant barriers to climate change adaptation. Limited resources are primarily directed toward basic needs, leaving little for disaster preparedness. Many are engaged in multiple jobs, limiting civic participation. This lack of engagement further hinders their ability to advocate for and access resources needed for effective disaster preparedness and response. Hurricane Irma highlighted these challenges, especially for those reliant on fixed incomes and state welfare (EBT), with a lack of liquid assets. Major concerns after the hurricane were food, water, and AC. Miami's high economic inequality exacerbates these disparities, underscoring the need for climate actions that support both resilience and equitable development. As of 2024, Miami has the 5th highest Gini Index (0.5546) in the United States. Based on 2023 ACS data, 17.9% of all residents live in poverty. A large portion of those living in poverty are children (21.7% of residents under 18) and older adults (29.3% of residents over 65). According to the 2023 United Way Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed (ALICE) report, 61% of Black households and 52% of Hispanic households in Miami-Dade County were below the ALICE Threshold, compared to 38% of White households. As such, issues of poverty and unequal development pose a crucial consideration for equitable adaptation. In addition, this reality highlights the importance of seeking co-benefits of climate actions which support equity and economic development.

column16:
Las opciones limitadas de movilidad promueven que la primer opción de transporte sea el vehículo privado, causando que la población invierta cada vez más tiempo en sus traslados. 

Actualmente la duración de un trayecto en transporte público en la Zona Metropolitana de Monterrey ha aumentado en los últimos dos años, pasando de un promedio de 62 a 66 minutos. Únicamente 13.14% de las personas realizan trayectos de 30 minutos o menos, 38.34% realizan trayectos de una a dos horas y 6.92% tienen trayectos mayores a dos horas en cada recorrido de ida o vuelta. 

Bajo este panorama, la calidad de vida y productividad de los habitantes se ve perjudicada. Asimismo, la infraestructura de transporte y movilidad actual limita la capacidad de adaptación ante eventos climáticos extremos. Lo anterior se observa en la posibilidad de que la población quede incomunicada, sin acceso a bienes, servicios, y a la respuesta ante emergencias.

El cambio climático contribuye directamente a emergencias humanitarias debido al incremento en frecuencia, intensidad y escala de fenómenos climáticos extremos, los cuales pueden afectar negativamente la salud humana. 

Las personas que están expuestas a temperaturas muy altas, pueden llegar a experimentar fatiga, debilidad, mareos, deshidratación y agotamiento por calor. Adicionalmente, durante las olas de calor la calidad del aire puede deteriorarse debido a la formación de contaminantes atmosféricos. 

Por otro lado, la presencia de frentes fríos en la Zona Metropolitana de Monterrey propicia la generación de inversiones térmicas, las cuales pueden provocar graves episodios de contaminación atmosféricos, los cuales afectan la salud de la población. 

Aunado a lo anterior, el cambio climático ha incrementado el área de distribución de las enfermedades transmitidas por vectores. En el caso de Nuevo León, los años de mayor ocurrencia de dengue clásico fueron 2013, 2017 y 2020, mientras que 2013 fue el año con mayor número de casos de dengue hemorrágico.

Las montañas que rodean la ciudad establecen límites naturales que son superados con la emergencia de asentamientos irregulares en zonas de alta pendiente; esta situación genera exposición de la población ante la ocurrencia de deslizamientos y otros eventos con detonantes meteorológicos.

La cuenca el río Aburrá en donde se localiza la ciudad es atravesada por afluente de alta torrencialidad, que bajo eventos de lluvia extrema, generan amenazas que pueden materializarse en desastres. Esta situación se verá acrecentada por el incremento de la intensidad y periodicidad de eventos extremos de precipitación. 

Por último, el contexto de valle, su gradiente altitudinal y la localización en la zona andina de Colombia genera que, durante cada cambio de temporada de menos a más lluvias se den fenómenos de estabilidad atmosférica que limitan la dispersión de contaminantes atmosféricos, incrementando los índices de contaminación del aire y afectando la salud de la población más vulnerable.

column16: Desde finales del siglo XX e inicios del XXI, Medellín ha avanzado en un proceso de transición económica que buscan consolidarle como ciudad de servicios. Esto ha permitido la emergencia de diferentes actividades económicas vinculadas a la innovación, el comercio, el turismo y la tecnología. El Producto Interno Bruto local se genera de manera diversa, sin mostrar prevalencia absoluta de algún tipo de actividad económica, para 2023 el comercio (13%), las actividades profesionales y de servicios (12,5%), las actividades inmobiliarias (8,5%) y las industrias manufactureras (10,5%) se disputaron el primer lugar en generación de valor agregado. \n\nEntre 2005 y 2022, la participación de las industrias manufactureras en el valor agregado a presentado una reducción progresiva, desde el 20,8 % en 2005 al 11,3% en 2022. En contrataste, sectores como actividades financieras, información y comunicaciones, actividades científicas y de servicios, servicios de alimentación y alojamiento y atención en salud han tenido un crecimiento constante. Esta diversidad se identifica como un factor altamente positivo para acelerar una transición económica verde, justa y resiliente.

Este sistema se apoya en diversas herramientas que han permitido el involucramiento decidido de la ciudadanía. La migración en Medellín es un fenómeno que debe analizarse desde diferentes perspectivas. De acuerdo con la Unidad para la Atención y Reparación Integral a las Víctimas para 31 de mayo de 2021 se identifican en Medellín 319.022 personas reconocidas como víctimas del desplazamiento forzado interno en el marco del conflicto armado, de acuerdo con la ley 1448 de 2011. Cifra que resulta dinámica debido a los continuos flujos de población generados por la presencia de grupos armados en zonas rurales del país. A las dificultades presentes, podría sumarse un flujo futuro de población afectada por los efectos del clima en zonas rurales y productivas del país. La tercera comunicación nacional de Cambio Climático estima que puede darse un aumento en la intensidad de los fenómenos de variabilidad climática, lo que afectará la productividad y habitabilidad de zonas rurales afectadas por las lluvias o sequías prolongadas. Medellín debe prepararse ante este escenario.

Por último, Migración Colombia (2024) estima que, para abril 30 de 2024, residen en Colombia cerca de 2.813.997 migrantes venezolanos, el 8,42 %, correspondiente a 237.021, habita Medellín para esta fecha, situación que ha significado un desafío creciente en materia de atención y que, probablemente, ha detonado la emergencia de nuevos asentamientos humanos en zonas de riesgo geológico.

La dinámica migratoria implica retos en la ampliación de la cobertura de programas sociales y la prevención de la emergencia de asentamientos expuestos a amenazas. Las características de desarraigo constituyen un condicionante de vulnerabilidad.

column16: Increases in housing cost, shortage in housing supply, and poverty have contributed to the rise in the City's homeless population. The Maricopa County homeless population point-in-time count indicates an increase in homelessness from 6,298 to 9,734 individuals for the years 2018 to 2025. These numbers represent a 54% increase (https://azmag.gov/Programs/Homelessness/Data/Point-In-Time-Homelessness-Count). Homeless individuals are highly susceptible to extreme heat mortality and morbidity due to continuous exposure to the extreme heat. The Phoenix Office of Heat Response and Mitigation, and Office of Homeless Solutions, work to provide cooling centers with air conditioning, as well as assistance to find homeless shelter beds and permanent housing. Creating and maintaining adequate housing for individuals is critical for addressing the homeless challenge. The City's Housing Plan 2030 has a goal of creating or preserving 50,000 housing units by the year 2030. As December 2024, Phoenix has exceeded this goal, by completing more than 53,000 housing units (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/housing-news/3341.html).

column16: The City initiated a Stage 1 Water Alert in June 2022 as part of the City's ongoing commitment to sustainable water management and in response to the shortage of water on the Colorado River affecting the region. This step is an integral component of the City's Drought Management Plan. Phoenix is asking for the community's cooperation in implementing voluntary water conservation measures. In 2025, Phoenix made the Mayor's “Save Water Pledge” an ongoing permanent initiative to continue the City's commitment to sustainability and water resiliency in the face of ongoing drought and climate challenges (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/supply-conservation/save-water/mayor-pledge.html). Healthy infrastructure is the foundation of a strong city -- which is why the City of Tampa launched the Progressive Infrastructure Plan to Ensure Sustainability (PIPES).

With PIPES, the City of Tampa is investing in Tampa's tomorrow and is moving forward with the largest public works project in the City's history, one that will transform the 100-year-old water and wastewater infrastructure that serves over 733,000 people. 

What is PIPES?
PIPES is $2.9 billion funding plan for large-scale sewer and water infrastructure improvements. It was passed by the Tampa City Council in September 2019 after nearly 10 years without a utility rate increase. The funding plan allows the City to adopt a proactive approach to renew our infrastructure, prevent breakdowns, and provide long-term, permanent fixes to our water and wastewater systems.

Key Facts
PIPES establishes a schedule of gradual rate increases for water and wastewater services over a 20 year period.
These increases will eventually align water and wastewater rates with the funding needed to catch up and continuously renew and replace infrastructure as it reaches the end of its useful life.
In addition to gradually raising usage (consumption) rates, PIPES also implemented a monthly base charge for water and wastewater services.
Tampa was one of the last municipalities in Florida to implement a base charge.

Integration of hierarchical solutions across the city.

Creation of a unified database and development of sensitivity maps.
Creation of a portfolio of innovative and available solutions, identifying opportunities for comprehensive runoff management in the urban space.

column16: Climate change is increasingly affecting Palermo's environment. Urban flooding triggered by extreme rainfall overwhelms drainage systems, leading to flash floods in streets and neighborhoods. Meanwhile, widespread drought and water scarcity on the island threaten agriculture, water supplies, and biodiversity, with over 70% of Sicily's territory at risk of desertification. Rising temperatures, more frequent heatwaves, and intense rainfall events expose weaknesses in the city's infrastructure, such as limited green spaces, aging drainage systems, and vulnerable housing in low-income areas. These environmental stressors demand rapid adaptation, yet Palermo struggles with limited financial resources and social inequality—factors that hinder coordinated climate response. While there are some local efforts and awareness campaigns, the city's ability to adapt effectively remains constrained without stronger institutional support and investment in climate-resilient planning.

column16:
A infraestrutura urbana é um dos setores críticos para a adaptação de Salvador às mudanças climáticas. Entre os elementos mais relevantes estão os sistemas de alerta e monitoramento, bem como as redes de esgotamento sanitário e drenagem pluvial. Essas estruturas desempenham papel fundamental na redução da vulnerabilidade da cidade frente a eventos extremos, como chuvas intensas e inundações.
As ações de monitoramento, alerta, educação e conscientização são coordenadas, principalmente, por meio do Projeto de Formação de Núcleos Comunitários de Proteção e Defesa Civil (NUPDEC), que atua em diversas áreas do município com foco na mobilização e preparação da população para situações de risco.
Além disso, os sistemas de esgoto, muitas vezes integrados aos sistemas de drenagem de águas pluviais, influenciam diretamente a capacidade da cidade de lidar com alagamentos. A eficiência dessas infraestruturas contribui para aumentar ou reduzir a sensibilidade das áreas urbanas às enchentes, especialmente em bairros com maior densidade populacional e baixa cobertura vegetal.
O fortalecimento e a expansão desses sistemas, aliados à participação comunitária e à gestão integrada do território, são fundamentais para tornar Salvador mais resiliente diante dos impactos climáticos crescentes.

column16: O acesso a serviços públicos básicos, como saúde, saneamento, habitação e assistência social, é considerado um fator essencial de capacidade adaptativa. Quanto maior o acesso a esses serviços, mais preparada estará a população para enfrentar e reduzir os impactos dos riscos climáticos, como picos de temperatura, deslizamentos de terra, enchentes e surtos de doenças. Regiões com melhor infraestrutura e maior cobertura desses serviços tendem a apresentar menores índices de vulnerabilidade, favorecendo respostas mais eficazes e seguras diante dos eventos extremos.

column16: Salvador é uma cidade costeira com alta densidade urbana, sendo 99,9% de seu território classificado como área urbana. A crise habitacional no município remonta à década de 1950, impulsionada pelo crescimento populacional decorrente da migração campo-cidade, somado à ausência de políticas habitacionais voltadas principalmente para as populações de baixa renda. Esse processo resultou em uma expansão acelerada da ocupação informal, marcada por invasões de terras públicas e privadas.\nSegundo dados de 2015 da Fundação Israel Pinheiro (FIJ), a Região Metropolitana de Salvador (RMS) apresentava, à época, um déficit habitacional estimado em cerca de 139 mil domicílios (FIJ, 2018). Esse quadro contribui para a ocupação irregular de áreas ambientalmente sensíveis e de risco, como Áreas de Preservação Permanente (APPs), nascentes, margens de cursos d'água e topos de morros.\nAs condições precárias de moradia em grande parte dessas áreas aumentam significativamente a vulnerabilidade socioambiental da população, expondo-a de forma mais intensa aos impactos das mudanças climáticas, como inundações, deslizamentos de terra e ondas de calor. O enfrentamento dessa realidade exige políticas públicas integradas de habitação, urbanização de assentamentos precários e adaptação climática, com foco na justiça social e territorial.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: O acesso aos serviços de saúde é um importante indicador de capacidade adaptativa, especialmente diante do aumento de doenças associadas ao clima, como aquelas transmitidas por vetores e os agravos relacionados às ondas de calor. Os vetores, como o Aedes aegypti, estão entre os primeiros organismos a responder aos efeitos das mudanças climáticas, devido à sua alta taxa de reprodução, rápida dispersão e curto ciclo de vida. Essas características facilitam surtos em áreas com condições propícias, especialmente em contextos de vulnerabilidade social e urbana.\nAlém disso, os picos de temperatura impactam diretamente a saúde humana, podendo agravar doenças crônicas, causar desidratação, insolação e aumento da mortalidade, especialmente entre idosos, crianças e pessoas com comorbidades. Por isso, quanto maior e mais equitativo for o acesso à rede de saúde, melhor preparada estará a população para prevenir, identificar e tratar os efeitos adversos das mudanças climáticas.

column16:
Os indicadores de capacidade adaptativa estão fortemente relacionados à condição socioeconômica da população e à presença de infraestrutura que favoreça uma resposta eficaz diante da ocorrência de eventos climáticos extremos. Nesse contexto, destaca-se o papel da renda média, pois ela permite que as pessoas adotem medidas preventivas, enfrentem melhor os impactos de desastres e recuperem-se mais rapidamente.
De acordo com o IBGE (2017), 44,8% da população da Bahia vive abaixo da linha da pobreza. Embora Salvador seja a capital mais desenvolvida do estado, ainda concentra 24,2% de sua população em situação de pobreza, o que representa aproximadamente 715 mil pessoas.
As doenças de veiculação hídrica, como a diarreia, estão diretamente associadas a fatores ambientais e socioeconômicos, incluindo a renda familiar, densidade domiciliar, escolaridade materna, acesso à água potável, destinação adequada de resíduos, local de moradia (urbano ou rural), além de condições nutricionais. Entre esses fatores, o acesso ao saneamento básico se destaca como um dos mais determinantes para a prevenção dessas enfermidades.
Segundo dados do IBGE (2010), Salvador possuía 92,8% dos domicílios com saneamento considerado adequado, mas apenas 35% das vias urbanas apresentavam urbanização completa, com bueiros, calçadas, pavimentação e meio-fio. Essa limitação na infraestrutura urbana agrava a vulnerabilidade da população, especialmente em áreas periféricas e de ocupação irregular.
Considerando a complexidade geomorfológica do município, a diversidade de sistemas meteorológicos que provocam chuvas intensas e a alta concentração de famílias de baixa renda em áreas de risco, Salvador registra um elevado número de desastres naturais, como inundações e deslizamentos, que afetam de forma desproporcional as populações mais vulneráveis.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16:
Salvador apresenta uma elevada desigualdade de renda. Em 2010, o município registrou um Índice de Gini de 0,63, um dos mais altos do país. De acordo com a PNAD Contínua (IBGE, 2019), os domicílios mais ricos da cidade possuem renda até 61 vezes maior do que os das famílias mais pobres. Essa disparidade é refletida também na configuração urbana: cerca de 32% da população vive em assentamentos informais, segundo o IBGE.
A renda é um dos fatores mais relevantes na definição da capacidade adaptativa da população frente aos riscos climáticos. Famílias com maior poder aquisitivo conseguem, por exemplo, investir em tecnologias de mitigação, como o uso de ar-condicionado durante ondas de calor, ou realizar obras de melhoria habitacional em áreas de risco. Já as populações de baixa renda permanecem mais expostas e vulneráveis a eventos extremos.
Outros indicadores de adaptação incluem as taxas de alfabetização de mulheres acima de 15 anos, um fator associado à tomada de decisão informada no ambiente familiar, e o acesso ao sistema de saúde, fundamental para a prevenção e resposta a emergências climáticas e sanitárias.
Diante desses desafios, a atual gestão municipal tem buscado promover o crescimento econômico inclusivo por meio de iniciativas sociais e de fortalecimento de capacidades locais. Entre elas, destacam-se a ampliação de Unidades de Saúde em bairros vulneráveis, o lançamento do edital Mulheres e Tecnologia, voltado à geração de renda e inclusão produtiva, e a criação do Centro de Inovação Social - COLABORE, espaço dedicado ao empreendedorismo de impacto social.

column16: Climate change drivers such as increase in ambient and seawater temperatures, heavy rain events and storm surges may impact the operations of Dubai's power and water sector resulting in a disruption across key sectors of the economy. The greatest concern is storm surge as more water is transported by winds, tides and waves can increase damage to electricity assets and reduce electricity supply. In response, the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) developed the Climate Change Resilience Plan in 2020, the first of its kind in the region which institutionalized climate adaptation by identifying climate risks and embedding them into DEWA's Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework. This integration enables proactive monitoring and planning for high-risk scenarios across infrastructure and supply systems. Until today, the plan has delivered tangible outcomes, including strengthened infrastructure resilience against climate-driven disruptions, improved operational continuity by reducing climate-induced service interruptions, and enhanced risk preparedness to ensure adaptive capacity for future climate uncertainties. column16: Since the 1990s, rapid urbanization centered around the Seoul Metropolitan Area has led to a significant increase in the population of Goyang City. When Goyang was elevated to city in 1992, its population was only 257,834, but by 2024, it had grown to 1,071,802 - an increase of more than four times in just 30 years. While population growth positively contributes to enhancing the city's competitiveness, it also leads to an increase in climate vulnerable groups, such as elderly, low-income households, and people with disabilities. Therefore, proactive measures must be taken to address these challenges.\nFirst, the increase in impervious surfaces in urban areas can lead to river flooding and sewer overflow during heavy rainfall. This, in turn, can cause road non-point source pollution and untreated sewage to flow into water system, leading to public health and water quality issues. Therefore, it is essential to systematically manage local rivers and establish a smooth urban water circulation system.\nSecond, while Goyang City is home to various rarity, urban development is damaging their primary habitats. For instance, the Janghang Wetland, located in the Han River estuary, is an 'ecological treasure' that hosts numerous rarity and serves as a stopover for migratory birds. However, recent urbanization and development have led to changes in species movement patterns, an increase in the invasion of alien species, and a decline in species due to climate change, all of which necessitate appropriate countermeasures.

column16: Zaragoza se encuentra en el centro de la Depresión del Ebro, una gran llanura en el noreste de la península ibérica, en la comunidad autónoma de Aragón. Esta depresión está flanqueada por los Pirineos al norte y el Sistema Ibérico al sur, lo que le da a la región unas características geográficas muy particulares. El clima de Zaragoza es mediterráneo con una marcada influencia continental. Esto se traduce en varias características climáticas. Veranos muy calurosos y secos, inviernos frío y secos, aunque no tan extremos como en otras regiones continentales, son fríos, con temperaturas que pueden bajar de los 0°C durante las noches. Baja pluviosidad, la precipitación anual media que ronda los 300 a 400 mm. La mayoría de las lluvias se concentran en otoño y primavera, pero incluso en estas estaciones, las precipitaciones suelen ser esporádicas y moderadas. Debido a la influencia continental, Zaragoza experimenta una gran diferencia entre las temperaturas diurnas y nocturnas, especialmente en primavera y otoño. Además, la amplitud térmica entre el invierno y el verano es también significativa. Además, se caracteriza por los vientos. El cierzo es un viento característico de la región, proveniente del noroeste. Sopla con bastante frecuencia, especialmente en otoño e invierno, y puede ser bastante fuerte y frío, influyendo notablemente en la sensación térmica de la ciudad. Estas características climáticas hacen que la adaptación al cambio climático sea cada vez más necesaria, especialmente en los periodos más calurosos del año, como se ha dicho en otros apartados

column16: The Municipality of Porto has ongoing projects and initiatives aimed at encouraging public participation and civil society involvement in solutions for mitigating and adapting to climate change. One of the most recent and pressing examples of this involvement is the Porto Climate Pact, which encourages citizens to actively participate in the co-creation of decarbonization policies, alongside various organizations in Porto. All key elements will be aligned within an ambitious plan towards climate positivity. Although we have been successful in fostering citizen participation and involvement in municipal projects, we recognize that there is still work to be done to ensure clear and consistent support, particularly when it comes to engaging specific sectors that may present challenges. Increasing public participation and stakeholder engagement in municipal projects has been a priority, but it remains a demanding and complex process. Furthermore, there is a notable deficit in climate literacy among the general population. To address this, the municipality is focusing on young students, schools, and companies as key target groups to boost climate literacy and foster greater engagement in climate change adaptation efforts across the community. In particular, we are deeply concerned about the most vulnerable segments of the population, such as low-income families, who may face additional barriers in accessing information and participating in climate initiatives. Therefore, we are developing tailored strategies to engage these groups, ensuring that they are not left behind in the transition to a sustainable future and are supported in adopting practices that contribute to both climate resilience and economic stability.

column16: The geography of the city is a limiting factor of the adaptation capacity, as it presents vulnerabilities inherent to these characteristics and geographical conditions, which almost surround the city. The clash with the sea to the west, with the Douro River to the south, and with the Tinto and Torto rivers to the east, create authentic natural borders, and constitute a risk itself, as coastal and river flooding, or even due to its very steep slopes. Due to these natural borders, the city is very dependent on the northern border in case of a catastrophic event, making it very vulnerable in terms of mobility or providing rescue or assistance. The morphology of the city, with high cliffs facing south, create constraints in the use and planning of the city. Also, the very consolidated coastline, the absence of primary dunes and the estuary of the Douro River, make the city very vulnerable to the rise in the average sea level, which in a small city like Porto, will have a considerable impact on the population, but mainly on the sectors and urban systems.
