Esses espaços contribuem para a melhoria da qualidade de vida da população, apoiam a segurança hídrica e promovem a resiliência ambiental, tornando-se aliados importantes na resposta aos desafios colocados pelas alterações climáticas.

column16: O fator “habitação” desafia a capacidade de adaptação do Município da Covilhã principalmente devido às vulnerabilidades associadas ao parque habitacional mais antigo, que pode não dispor de sistemas adequados de aquecimento ou arrefecimento, aumentando a exposição da população a desconfortos térmicos causados por ondas de calor ou frio intenso. Além disso, a existência de habitações arrendadas pode limitar investimentos em melhorias adaptativas, e a desigualdade no acesso a habitação de qualidade pode agravar a vulnerabilidade social, especialmente em freguesias com maior taxa de desemprego e menor nível de instrução, dificultando a capacidade de resposta às alterações climáticas.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Por outro lado, a habitação dá suporte moderado à capacidade de adaptação na medida em que existem freguesias no Concelho onde a vulnerabilidade habitacional é inferior à média, refletindo melhores condições do parque habitacional, como a presença de sistemas de climatização adequados e maior propriedade das habitações, que permitem reduzir o impacto das alterações climáticas. Essa melhoria na qualidade habitacional contribui para uma maior resiliência da população, facilitando a adaptação a novas condições ambientais e minimizando os riscos associados ao clima extremo.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: A desigualdade no Município da Covilhã representa um fator de desafio significativo à capacidade de adaptação às alterações climáticas. O PAESC identifica várias freguesias com elevada vulnerabilidade social, nomeadamente Verdelhos, Vale Formoso e Aldeia do Souto, Peraboa e Cortes do Meio, onde se registam maiores taxas de desemprego e menores níveis de escolaridade. Estas desigualdades limitam a capacidade das populações de aceder a informação, de aplicar medidas de mitigação ou adaptação, e de investir na melhoria das suas condições habitacionais ou no uso eficiente de energia. Adicionalmente, as populações mais idosas e mais jovens são particularmente vulneráveis, tanto pelas suas necessidades específicas como pela sua menor capacidade de resposta a eventos climáticos extremos. Assim, a desigualdade territorial e socioeconómica agrava o risco e compromete a resiliência do território, tornando a adaptação mais difícil e desigual.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Apesar de a desigualdade constituir um desafio dominante, existem zonas do Município da Covilhã com melhores indicadores sociais e económicos que contribuem para fortalecer a capacidade de adaptação. Freguesias como Covilhã e Canhoso, Boidobra, Ferro e Tortosendo apresentam percentagens mais elevadas de população com ensino superior, o que, segundo o PAESC, está associado a uma maior literacia climática e, por consequência, a uma maior capacidade de acesso à informação e implementação de medidas de adaptação. Estas disparidades internas permitem, em certa medida, a concentração de esforços e recursos em áreas com maior capacidade de ação e resposta, funcionando como núcleos de suporte para estratégias de adaptação mais amplas e integradas no concelho. Contudo, esse suporte é limitado quando comparado com o impacto geral da desigualdade nas zonas mais vulneráveis.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: As condições e a manutenção da infraestrutura no Município da Covilhã colocam desafios moderados à sua capacidade de adaptação às alterações climáticas. Grande parte do parque edificado é composto por construções anteriores a 1960, com materiais e técnicas menos eficientes, sobretudo nas freguesias de Teixoso e Sarzedo, Cantar-Galo e Vila do Carvalho, Boidobra e Tortosendo. Estes edifícios apresentam menor resistência a fenómenos climáticos extremos, como ondas de calor, chuvas intensas ou variações sazonais de temperatura. A reduzida presença de sistemas de arrefecimento, particularmente em áreas com maior densidade populacional e edifícios envelhecidos, acentua a vulnerabilidade ao calor. Além disso, a baixa eficiência energética de parte das infraestruturas existentes compromete a sua capacidade de mitigação e resposta rápida a riscos climáticos, dificultando a resiliência global do concelho.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Apesar dos desafios, algumas características das infraestruturas da Covilhã oferecem suporte moderado à adaptação climática. O concelho possui uma taxa elevada de alojamentos com sistemas de aquecimento (entre 89% e 98%), o que contribui para uma menor vulnerabilidade a temperaturas mínimas extremas, frequentemente associadas a fenómenos de frio intenso. Adicionalmente, existe uma cobertura significativa de alojamentos próprios, o que facilita intervenções estruturais por parte dos proprietários para melhorar a resiliência dos edifícios. O município conta ainda com centros de produção de energia eólica e hídrica, e um elevado potencial para energia solar, dadas as mais de 2.000 horas de sol por ano e uma radiação global anual elevada, o que constitui uma infraestrutura energética com margem para evolução sustentável e suporte à transição climática.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: O ordenamento do território no Município da Covilhã apresenta desafios relevantes à adaptação climática, particularmente devido à ocupação desordenada do solo, à dispersão de infraestruturas e à expansão urbana pouco integrada com os ecossistemas naturais. A existência de áreas urbanas com fraca integração de critérios de resiliência, zonas de risco (como encostas sujeitas a instabilidade ou áreas suscetíveis a cheias) ocupadas por edificações, e a insuficiente articulação entre as políticas de uso do solo e as dinâmicas climáticas previstas, limitam a capacidade do território de responder eficazmente aos impactos das alterações climáticas. Estes fatores dificultam, por exemplo, o controlo da impermeabilização dos solos, a gestão do risco de incêndio florestal e a proteção dos recursos hídricos, comprometendo uma adaptação territorial sustentável e segura.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Por outro lado, o ordenamento do território também dá suporte à adaptação climática ao integrar, em alguns instrumentos de planeamento e gestão territorial, diretrizes de mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas. A existência de planos municipais como o PMAC e o PAESC demonstra um esforço em alinhar as decisões territoriais com os riscos climáticos identificados, promovendo uma ocupação mais racional do solo, a proteção de áreas sensíveis e a valorização dos espaços verdes e infraestruturas sustentáveis. A consideração da variabilidade climática na definição de usos do solo e na priorização de intervenções por freguesia com maior vulnerabilidade evidencia o potencial do ordenamento do território como ferramenta estratégica para reduzir riscos e aumentar a resiliência do município face às alterações climáticas.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: A saúde pública no Município da Covilhã enfrenta desafios significativos no contexto das alterações climáticas, sobretudo devido à vulnerabilidade de grupos populacionais mais sensíveis, como idosos, crianças e pessoas com doenças crónicas. Os documentos do PMAC e PAESC identificam riscos acrescidos associados a ondas de calor, temperaturas extremas e eventos meteorológicos severos, que aumentam a incidência de doenças respiratórias, cardiovasculares e o risco de mortalidade prematura. A maior vulnerabilidade social em algumas freguesias, com limitações no acesso a cuidados de saúde adequados, agrava a exposição e reduz a capacidade de resposta a situações de emergência climática, comprometendo a resiliência do sistema de saúde pública local.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Apesar dos desafios, a saúde pública também oferece suporte moderado à adaptação climática no município, através da existência de estruturas básicas de atendimento, serviços médicos instalados e campanhas de sensibilização e educação para a saúde. A capacidade de resposta institucional, aliada a programas de vigilância e prevenção, contribui para a mitigação de impactos climáticos na saúde das populações. A integração da saúde como setor prioritário nas estratégias de adaptação (identificada no PAESC) reforça a importância da articulação entre saúde e ambiente, promovendo uma abordagem preventiva e mais resiliente face às alterações climáticas.

column16: A capacidade técnica no Município da Covilhã enfrenta alguns desafios que condicionam a eficácia da adaptação às alterações climáticas. Apesar do esforço de planeamento demonstrado na elaboração do PMAC e do PAESC, a execução plena das medidas propostas pode ser dificultada por limitações ao nível de recursos humanos especializados, falta de formação contínua em matérias climáticas e ambientais, e dificuldades na transversalização técnica do conhecimento entre departamentos. Além disso, a complexidade crescente das questões climáticas exige competências técnicas multidisciplinares e atualizadas, que nem sempre estão disponíveis internamente, levando à dependência de consultorias externas e atrasando processos de decisão e implementação.

column16: Por outro lado, o Município da Covilhã demonstra possuir uma base técnica relevante que dá suporte à sua capacidade de adaptação. A própria existência de instrumentos como o PMAC e o PAESC evidencia um nível de maturidade técnica e institucional importante. A recolha de dados, a identificação de setores vulneráveis, o uso de indicadores de risco climático e a definição de medidas específicas para mitigação e adaptação demonstram que há conhecimento técnico aplicado. Além disso, a colaboração com entidades externas, universidades e especialistas locais permite colmatar algumas lacunas internas e reforçar a capacidade técnica disponível para planear e responder aos desafios climáticos de forma mais integrada.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: A segurança hídrica representa um desafio significativo para a capacidade de adaptação do Município da Covilhã às alterações climáticas. Segundo o PAESC, os recursos hídricos do concelho apresentam uma elevada sensibilidade às secas, à redução da precipitação e às alterações sazonais do clima. Estes fatores aumentam o risco de escassez de água para consumo humano, agrícola e industrial, especialmente perante a maior frequência e intensidade de fenómenos extremos, como ondas de calor e períodos prolongados de seca. O PMAC também evidencia que o concelho possui áreas vulneráveis, onde a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos é agravada por infraestruturas deficitárias ou envelhecidas. Além disso, a dependência de regimes pluviais instáveis e a pressão sobre ecossistemas hídricos naturais afetam negativamente a capacidade de resposta em situações de stress hídrico.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Apesar dos desafios, o Município da Covilhã possui algumas condições que contribuem para dar suporte à segurança hídrica e, por conseguinte, à sua capacidade de adaptação. O concelho tem identificado, nos seus planos estratégicos, zonas de elevado valor ecológico que funcionam como áreas de proteção dos recursos hídricos, nomeadamente zonas florestais e áreas naturais com capacidade de retenção e infiltração de água. Além disso, o reconhecimento da vulnerabilidade hídrica nas políticas locais permite orientar investimentos para a melhoria da eficiência dos sistemas de abastecimento e saneamento, promovendo a redução de perdas de água e o uso eficiente deste recurso. Estas ações, conjugadas com a potencial implementação de medidas de adaptação, como o aproveitamento de águas pluviais e o aumento da resiliência da rede, contribuem para reforçar a segurança hídrica a médio e longo prazo.

Bradford District's ability to adapt to climate change is closely tied to its budgetary capacity, which presents both opportunities and constraints. On the supportive side, Bradford Council has made strategic investments in sustainability projects—such as the Clean Air Zone, low-carbon transport infrastructure, and the development of a district heat network—that demonstrate a commitment to climate resilience and innovation. These initiatives are backed by regional partnerships, including the Leeds City Region Climate Coalition, which aim to unlock funding and drive clean growth across West Yorkshire.

However, financial limitations remain a significant challenge. Like many local authorities, Bradford faces competing demands on its budget, with social care, education, and housing often taking precedence. This can restrict the scale and speed of climate adaptation measures, particularly in deprived communities where vulnerability to climate impacts is highest. The Council's Climate Action Plan 2025-2028 (https://www.bradford.gov.uk/media/bm3ps2mc/cbmdcclimateactionplan.pdf) acknowledges the need for external investment, cross-sector collaboration, and community-led action to bridge funding gaps and ensure equitable adaptation.

In essence, while Bradford has laid strong foundations for climate action, its budgetary constraints mean that sustained progress will depend on securing long-term funding, leveraging regional and national support, and embedding climate priorities across all areas of public spending.

Policy Disruption and Delays Climate adaptation requires consistent, long-term strategies—like those outlined in Bradford's 2025-2028 Climate Action Plan. Political instability, such as frequent leadership changes or council disputes, can derail these plans, delay implementation, or lead to shifting priorities.

Reduced Investor Confidence Uncertainty in governance can deter private and regional investment in green infrastructure, clean energy, and climate innovation. Projects like the Low Carbon Hydrogen initiative or the Mass Transit Tram System rely on stable partnerships and funding streams.

Fragmented Decision-Making Instability may lead to siloed departments, poor coordination, and weakened collaboration with regional bodies like the West Yorkshire Combined Authority. This fragmentation slows down integrated responses to climate threats like flooding or heatwaves.

Public Distrust and Low Engagement If residents perceive local politics as unstable or ineffective, they may disengage from climate consultations and community-led initiatives. Bradford's Climate Action Plan depends heavily on public participation to shape equitable and inclusive adaptation.

Vulnerability to Populist Backlash In times of political unrest, climate policies can become scapegoats—especially if they're perceived as costly or disruptive. This can lead to rollbacks in sustainability measures or resistance to necessary changes.

column16: Inequality significantly challenges Bradford District's ability to adapt to climate change, as the most deprived communities often face the greatest exposure to climate risks while having the least capacity to respond. Areas with lower income, poor housing quality, and limited access to green space are more vulnerable to flooding, heatwaves, and air pollution—issues already prevalent in parts of Bradford. These inequalities mean that adaptation strategies must go beyond infrastructure and include social support, inclusive planning, and targeted investment. On the supportive side, Bradford Council has acknowledged these disparities in its Climate Action Plan and is working to embed equity into its climate response, including through community-led initiatives and the Community Climate Fund, which aims to deliver significant funding to local community organisations by 2030. However, unless inequality is directly addressed—through better housing, access to clean energy, and inclusive decision-making—climate adaptation risks deepening existing divides rather than bridging them.

column16: Downtown Fredericton lies in a floodplain at the bottom of a hill. The city has historically experienced spring river flooding and is now experiencing heavy rainfall inundation. Históricamente el acceso a servicios de transporte en Monteverde ha sido escaso y en temporadas inexistente. Esto, combinado con otros factores tales como las características topográficas del cantón, las distancias de desplazamiento de los habitantes hacia sus trabajos, lugares de estudio, etc., las condiciones climatológicas y el alto costo en transporte privado, ha significado un reto en la movilidad de la población y por consecuencia la capacidad de adaptación de la población. 

Actualmente el cantón cuenta con un solo bus público interurbano ofreciendo una única ruta cuatro veces por día. Ante esta baja cobertura, la población recurre a otras alternativas de movilización como; caminar, motocicleta, vehículo propio, etc. Según un estudio socioeconómico realizado en 2022 (Encuesta comunitaria, 2022) únicamente un 19% de la población utiliza el transporte público como su medio de transporte principal mientras que el 59% se moviliza en su propio vehículo y el 65% lo hace caminando. Solo un 20% de la población indica tener problemas de acceso al transporte (Encuesta comunitaria, 2022). A pesar de que la mayor parte de la población logra cubrir sus necesidades de movilidad, la dependencia en el transporte privado presenta un desafío para grupos poblaciones vulnerables que no logran acceder al mismo, tales como las infancias, adultos mayores y población de bajos recursos. Generalmente estos son los grupos más afectados por los desastres naturales, y quienes ante cualquier evento necesitarán más acceso a transporte para desplazarse según sea necesario. 

Por otro lado en los últimos años se han construido cantidad significativa de metros en aceras aumentando la accesibilidad y seguridad para los peatones y formando una red de aceras que permitan a más personas movilizarse caminando. Adicionalmente se han trabajado en diferentes proyectos de transporte colectivo que aumenten la accesibilidad al transporte para los habitantes y, a su vez, disminuyan la cantidad de vehículos (ridesharing, carpooling, transporte colectivo de turismo, entre otros). A través de estas diferentes actividades se busca sobrepasar estos desafíos mencionados y aumentar el acceso a movilidad de la población.

Accessing data that is reliable, consistent and in the format that enables effective planning and decision-making is a challenge for work on climate change at the sub-national level. This is a challenge for mitigation work but also for adaptation and resilience. We need to be able to make a case for investment based on good quality data. The WMCA's Environment and Net Zero Data Dashboard has sort to address data limitations and provides a one-stop-shop for climate data, including the WMCA's CRVA at lower super output area (LSOA) scale.

The lack of severe weather impact data for the region makes it difficult for organisations to understand how they're currently being affected by climate hazards and to project these risks into future climate scenarios. The WMCA are working with the Local Resilience Forum to establish a mechanism for recording the impacts of severe weather events on member organisations. In the mid-long term, this will help the region monitor resilience and adaptation outcomes. However, it takes time and organizational willingness to build this database and to record incident impacts in a consistent way. 

Organisations currently lack data on their levels of adaptive capacity. The WMCA are working with Climate Sense to administer their Capacity Diagnosis and Development (CaDD) tool to Regional Adaptation Network (RAN) members. This is a survey that scores organisations for their respective levels of adaptive capacity. This progress in monitoring adaptive capacity will give the WMCA a picture of adaptive capacity levels across the region. The success of these adaptive capacity assessments and the breadth of data collected through them is dependent on the uptake of the survey itself.

There are significant challenges in relation to poverty in the West Midlands: 1) In the West Midlands, 20% of people lived in a household that is below the relative low income line (bringing in less than 60% of today's average income).2) For children the rate is even higher - 26% of children are in families classed as living in poverty.3) 304,000 households are currently living in fuel poverty. In the light of the current cost of living crisis and rising fuel bills, it is expected this figure will rise. Only 35% of homes in the West Midlands are rated EPC band C and above. This is a challenge, but is also pointing us to where we need to prioritise, for example in terms of the roll out of a regional retrofit programme.

The West Midlands Climate Risk & Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA) includes several layers of socio-economic data, indicating which communities are vulnerable to the climate hazards due to their limited capacity and resources to deal with and bounce back from them when they occur. The WMCA considers factors like deprivation, low levels of disposable income and lack of access to private vehicles all as components that could limit an individuals' capacity to adapt to climate change. This, combined with proximity to climate hazards, indicates where adaptation might disproportionately impact different communities and therefore where the organisation should be focusing efforts to build adaptive capacity.

There are serious limitations in resourcing this work. Both the WMCA and its constituent authorities often lack the capacity (both revenue and capital budgets) to plan and deliver climate adaptation solutions. While the WMCA have conducted its own climate risk assessment and adaptation plan (under adaptation reporting - ARP4), there are limitations in the budget and human resources available to work on adaptation. There are also no statutory responsibilities nor formal mandates that drive forward investment in adaptation.

The WMCA has been able to finance the recruitment of a Climate Adaptation Project Manager, who has been in post since 2023. The project manager supports local authority officers and team across the WMCA where their own adaptive capacity is limited. The project manager also builds constructive partnerships with organisations across the region to secure funding - one example being the £2m UKRI-funded WM-Adapt project, funding for which was secured through partnership working between the WMCA, the University of Birmingham and the Birmingham Voluntary Service Council. The bidding for individual pots of grant funding, which last only a few years and then come to an end, requires significant human resource to work on applications and the build these relationships. This approach to resourcing climate adaptation and building adaptive capacity is not sustainable but it is the most effective approach that the WMCA currently has without any devolved responsibility and resources for adaptation planning and delivery. 

There is still a wider issue of a lack of budget to deliver. On a broader scale, funding is required across the Net- Zero workstreams of the WMCA; implementation of the first Five Year Plan is expected to require 4.3 bn.

column16: The adaptive capacity of George Municipality to manage climate hazards such as droughts, urban flooding, coastal flooding, biodiversity loss and wildfire risks is significantly challenged by the accessibility and quality of data. A critical issue is the absence of localised monitoring systems to record the frequency, severity and impacts of these climate events. Without these systems, the municipality primarily relies on provincial and district-level data, which is often too broad and not sufficiently detailed to inform the specific needs of each ward in the municipality. The lack of local monitoring means that George Municipality cannot accurately assess the unique risks it faces. For example, without real-time data on drought conditions or rainfall patterns specific to the municipality, it becomes difficult to manage water resources effectively. Similarly, urban and coastal flooding risks are harder to predict without detailed topographical data and real-time storm tracking, making it challenging to implement infrastructure that is resilient to these hazards. Furthermore, the data available at the provincial and district levels may not be at the appropriate scale for effective decision-making within the municipality. This misalignment can result in strategies that do not adequately address the specific vulnerabilities of George. For example, provincial data provide general trends in temperature increases, but without granular information on local microclimates, the municipality's efforts to manage wildfire risks or protect biodiversity could be misdirected or insufficient.

column16: The technical capacity of George Municipality, particularly in terms of dedicated staff for climate change planning presents a moderate challenge to fully integrating climate change impacts into municipal planning. One of the key issues is that the municipality does not have a sufficient number of staff specifically trained and dedicated to addressing climate change. This shortage means that existing staff must take on climate-related tasks in addition to their regular duties. This can lead to a lack of focus and depth in addressing climate risks, as climate change planning requires specialised knowledge and continuous attention to evolving data and trends. The reliance on external sources for climate modelling and data interpretation can also lead to a disconnect between the data provided and the specific needs of George Municipality. External consultants may not fully understand the local context or may not be available to provide ongoing support, which is critical for adaptive management in response to new climate information.

column16: Budget constraints is a significant challenge for George Municipality when it comes to addressing climate change impacts. The municipal budget is primarily allocated for service delivery which address baseline challenges, such as maintaining and improving essential services like water supply, sanitation, infrastructure, and waste management. Climate change introduces an additional layer of complexity and financial burden that stretches the already limited resources of the municipality. As the impacts of climate change become more pronounced—through increased risks of drought, flooding, coastal erosion, biodiversity loss, and wildfires—the municipality is faced with the need to invest in adaptation and mitigation measures. However, these climate-related initiatives often require significant upfront investment in new infrastructure, technology, and human resources. Given that most of the municipal budget is provisioned for service delivery, there is limited financial flexibility to allocate funds specifically for climate change adaptation and mitigation. This means that the municipality is unable to timeously implement necessary measures such as upgrading drainage systems to cope with increased flooding, reinforcing coastal defences, investing in wildfire prevention and management strategies or improving water conservation efforts during droughts.

A cidade de Cáceres enfrenta desafios significativos na adaptação às mudanças climáticas, e um dos principais obstáculos é a falta de capacidade de infraestrutura. Essa limitação impacta diretamente a resiliência da comunidade, exacerbando os riscos associados a eventos climáticos extremos, como secas, enchentes e ondas de calor.

As deficiências na infraestrutura urbana, como a presença de estradas não pavimentadas, sistemas de drenagem inadequados e a falta de um sistema de esgoto eficiente, dificultam a capacidade da cidade de responder efetivamente às mudanças climáticas. Estradas não pavimentadas se tornam intransitáveis em períodos de chuva, isolando comunidades e dificultando o acesso a serviços essenciais. Durante chuvas intensas, a ineficácia dos sistemas de drenagem resulta em alagamentos, colocando em risco a vida e a propriedade dos cidadãos. Além disso, a ausência de parques lineares e áreas verdes limita a capacidade da cidade de mitigar o calor extremo, afetando a saúde da população.

Essas vulnerabilidades também têm implicações sociais e econômicas. Comunidades mais pobres, que frequentemente habitam áreas mais suscetíveis a desastres, são desproporcionalmente afetadas por eventos climáticos adversos. A perda de bens e a interrupção de serviços essenciais podem levar a um ciclo de pobreza e exclusão social, dificultando ainda mais a recuperação após desastres.

Para enfrentar esses desafios, é crucial que Cáceres invista em melhorias de infraestrutura que sejam resilientes às mudanças climáticas. Isso inclui o fortalecimento dos sistemas de drenagem, a pavimentação das estradas, a criação de parques lineares e a implementação de um sistema de esgoto adequado. Além disso, promover um planejamento urbano sustentável e garantir a participação da comunidade nas decisões de desenvolvimento são fundamentais para construir uma cidade mais resiliente.

Assim, a falta de capacidade de infraestrutura em Cáceres não é apenas um obstáculo; é uma oportunidade para repensar o desenvolvimento urbano. Ao priorizar a adaptação às mudanças climáticas, a cidade pode garantir um futuro mais seguro e sustentável para todos os seus habitantes. Mobilizar recursos, fortalecer parcerias e engajar a comunidade são ações essenciais para transformar essa visão em realidade.

column16:
A falta de mobilidade urbana adequada tem um impacto significativo na adaptação às mudanças climáticas, afetando a resiliência das comunidades e a eficiência das respostas às crises climáticas. Em primeiro lugar, a mobilidade inadequada pode limitar o acesso da população a serviços essenciais, como saúde, educação e assistência em situações de emergência. Sem meios de transporte confiáveis, as pessoas podem ter dificuldade em chegar a hospitais ou centros de atendimento durante desastres climáticos, aumentando a vulnerabilidade da comunidade.

Além disso, a falta de um sistema de transporte eficiente geralmente resulta em congestionamento e aumento das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. Isso agrava os problemas de qualidade do ar, que afetam a saúde da população e podem tornar a comunidade menos resiliente a eventos climáticos extremos. A dependência de veículos particulares, comum em áreas com mobilidade urbana deficiente, não só contribui para a poluição, mas também dificulta a implementação de soluções de transporte sustentável, como ônibus e bicicletas, que poderiam reduzir a pegada de carbono da cidade.

Outro aspecto importante é a inequidade social. A falta de opções de transporte acessível e eficiente pode acentuar desigualdades, com comunidades marginalizadas sendo as mais afetadas. Isso limita a capacidade dessas comunidades de se adaptar às mudanças climáticas e de participar em processos de tomada de decisão.

Além disso, um sistema de mobilidade urbana inadequado pode dificultar a implementação de políticas de adaptação, como a criação de zonas de proteção contra inundações ou a construção de infraestruturas resilientes. Se as pessoas não conseguem se deslocar facilmente, a execução dessas políticas se torna mais complicada. Por último, a mobilidade ineficiente pode impactar negativamente a economia local, dificultando o acesso ao trabalho e reduzindo a produtividade. Em tempos de crise climática, isso pode limitar os recursos disponíveis para iniciativas de adaptação e mitigação.

Em suma, a falta de mobilidade urbana adequada prejudica a adaptação às mudanças climáticas de várias maneiras, tornando as comunidades mais vulneráveis e limitando sua capacidade de se preparar e responder a desafios climáticos. Investir em um sistema de transporte eficiente e sustentável é essencial para fortalecer a resiliência das cidades e garantir um futuro mais seguro para todos os seus habitantes.

A falta de capacidade orçamentária é um fator crítico que afeta a adaptação às mudanças climáticas de diversas maneiras. Primeiramente, sem recursos financeiros adequados, é difícil realizar investimentos necessários em infraestrutura resiliente, como sistemas de drenagem, proteção costeira e áreas verdes. Essa carência de infraestrutura pode aumentar a vulnerabilidade das comunidades a eventos climáticos extremos.

Além disso, a escassez de orçamento pode levar à redução ou até mesmo à eliminação de programas e serviços essenciais voltados para a adaptação climática, como educação ambiental, serviços de saúde preventiva e assistência a agricultores para práticas agrícolas sustentáveis. Sem recursos, a implementação efetiva de políticas públicas que abordem as mudanças climáticas torna-se um desafio, resultando em estagnação nas iniciativas de adaptação.

A falta de recursos financeiros também dificulta a realização de pesquisas e o desenvolvimento de inovações necessárias para entender melhor as mudanças climáticas e identificar soluções adaptativas eficazes. A ausência de dados pode prejudicar a tomada de decisões informadas, tornando as estratégias de adaptação menos eficazes.

Adicionalmente, os grupos mais vulneráveis, que frequentemente dependem de serviços públicos, são os mais afetados pela escassez orçamentária. Isso pode aumentar as desigualdades sociais e dificultar a adaptação de comunidades carentes. A falta de capacidade orçamentária também pode atrasar a resposta a desastres climáticos, resultando em maiores danos e custos a longo prazo, já que os recursos escassos limitam a capacidade de mobilização e resposta rápida em situações de crise.

Por fim, governos com orçamentos limitados podem ter dificuldade em atrair investimentos externos, como financiamentos internacionais para projetos de adaptação, que muitas vezes exigem contrapartidas financeiras. Em resumo, a falta de capacidade orçamentária prejudica a adaptação às mudanças climáticas em múltiplas frentes, tornando as comunidades mais vulneráveis e limitando sua capacidade de se preparar e responder a desafios climáticos. A alocação adequada de recursos financeiros é, portanto, fundamental para fortalecer a resiliência e garantir um futuro mais seguro e sustentável.

The data currently available to us leaves a number of gaps in our knowledge that would assist planning for adaptation, including data about climate risks, the impacts of measures and the cost of inaction. 

This includes data about risk factors for health, such as the quantifiable relationship between rising temperatures and ill health. It also includes risk factors for the built environment that would help us model which buildings are most prone to unsafe indoor temperatures during heatwaves. Better data on the benefits of adaptation measures, such as the impact of tree planting on the Urban Heat Island, is needed. More data is also needed on the costs and impacts of failure to adapt.

The Climate Risk Assessment undertaken by H&F Council helps to address some of these knowledge gaps by providing recent data about local climate risks, e.g., which areas, populations and sectors are most vulnerable.

The region is challenged by multiple complex water quality issues. These include increased pollutant-loaded runoff, a growing list of water impairments, contaminated drinking water sources, and high costs for water treatment, utility operations, and infrastructure. The severity and type of contamination impacts how Minnesotans use and value the state's waters. The sources of contamination are both natural and caused by human activities. Uncertainty around emerging contaminants, regulatory changes, and climate change intensifies these issues, and complicates how to address water contamination. Holistic, proactive approaches and sound water policies are needed so that the region's waters can meet the region's needs. 

Currently, there are 802 water quality impairments in 451 river sections, lakes, or stream reaches in the metro region, with many waters having more than one impairment. Likewise, management and regulation of water usage has advanced significantly in recent decades leading to improved preparedness and resilience, fewer conflicts, improved coordination, and a greater understanding of water sustainability.  

The Met Council works with its partners towards the shared goal of safe, sustainable, and sufficient drinking water for the region. Source waters are the rivers, lakes, and aquifers that supply public drinking water systems and private wells. Source water protection is the suite of water quantity and quality actions and policies aimed to protect drinking water from pollution. Public water suppliers and the Minnesota Department of Health are responsible for providing safe drinking water, but they cannot protect drinking water supplies on their own. The Minnesota Department of Health works with public water suppliers, local decision-makers, other state agencies, and partner organizations like the Met Council to plan and implement activities that protect drinking water sources.

'Uno de los principales desafíos es la adaptación de la infraestructura a los efectos del cambio climático. El aumento de las temperaturas y el derretimiento de los glaciares pueden provocar inundaciones y deslizamientos de tierra, lo que exige la construcción de sistemas de drenaje y contención adecuados. Además, es necesario garantizar el acceso a agua potable y energía en un contexto de cambios ambientales.

Otro desafío importante es el crecimiento urbano acelerado, que demanda la expansión y mejora de la infraestructura de transporte, vivienda y servicios básicos. La construcción de nuevas rutas, la ampliación de la red de transporte público y la creación de viviendas adecuadas son fundamentales para garantizar la movilidad y el bienestar de la población.

La ubicación de Ushuaia también plantea desafíos logísticos para la construcción y el mantenimiento de la infraestructura. El transporte de materiales y equipos puede ser costoso y demorado, lo que exige una planificación cuidadosa y la búsqueda de soluciones locales.

Además, las condiciones climáticas extremas, como las bajas temperaturas y las fuertes nevadas, pueden dañar la infraestructura y dificultar su mantenimiento. Es necesario utilizar materiales y técnicas de construcción resistentes al frío y garantizar la disponibilidad de recursos para hacer frente a las contingencias climáticas.

Para superar estos desafíos, es fundamental invertir en investigación y desarrollo de tecnologías adaptadas a las condiciones locales, así como promover la participación de la comunidad en la planificación y gestión de la infraestructura. La colaboración entre el sector público y privado, así como el intercambio de conocimientos con otras ciudades y regiones, también son clave para encontrar soluciones innovadoras y sostenibles.

En resumen, los desafíos modernos de la infraestructura en Ushuaia son complejos y multifacéticos, pero pueden ser abordados mediante una planificación estratégica, inversiones adecuadas y la adopción de soluciones innovadoras y sostenibles.'

'En Ushuaia, la obtención de datos públicos ha sido históricamente un desafío, pero se han logrado avances significativos gracias a la modernización del Estado Municipal

La implementación de nuevas tecnologías y la digitalización de procesos han facilitado el acceso a la información pública. Se han creado plataformas en línea donde los ciudadanos pueden consultar datos sobre diversos temas, como presupuesto, obras públicas y estadísticas municipales.

Además, se ha promovido la transparencia y la rendición de cuentas, lo que ha contribuido a mejorar la calidad y la disponibilidad de los datos públicos. Se han establecido mecanismos de participación ciudadana para que los habitantes puedan involucrarse en la toma de decisiones y acceder a información relevante para la comunidad.

Si bien aún existen desafíos en cuanto a la disponibilidad y la calidad de los datos públicos, es importante reconocer los avances logrados en Ushuaia. La modernización del Estado ha sido fundamental para garantizar el acceso a la información y promover la participación ciudadana en la gestión de los asuntos públicos.

En el futuro, es fundamental seguir trabajando en la mejora de la calidad y la disponibilidad de los datos públicos, así como en la promoción de la transparencia y la rendición de cuentas. De esta manera, se fortalecerá la democracia y se garantizará el acceso a la información para todos los ciudadanos de Ushuaia. https://www.ushuaia.gob.ar/transparencia/'

However, Gainesville's location in Florida exposes it to the risks associated with tropical storms, hurricanes, and heavy rainfall events. While these weather events pose challenges, they can also serve as drivers for adaptation. By recognizing the vulnerability to extreme weather and implementing measures such as improved building codes, infrastructure resilience, and emergency response systems, Gainesville can enhance its ability to adapt to risks.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster has a high level of population as people enter and leave the city rapidly. Every year over 20,000 people leave and approximately the same number of new people move in. This high level of population turnover can make it more difficult for people to find and access services and for services to deliver the best outcomes. Demand for housing is high. The majority of people live in rented accommodation (both private and social housing) . People living in rented accommodation can be more exposed to changes in housing costs and the potential to experience deprivation and poverty than people who own their own homes. Westminster has the highest recorded population of rough sleepers of any local authority in the country. This population has higher rates of physical and mental health problems compared to the general population, and are at higher risk of complicating alcohol and or drug dependency. Rough sleepers attend accident and emergency approximately seven times more often than the general population, and are also subject to emergency admission and prolonged hospital stays more often.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster faces similar challenges to all UK local authorities, in that demand for many statutory services (particularly in Adults and Childrens Services) is growing year on year, whilst revenue support from central government to local authorities has fallen by £1.6 billion between 2010 and 2020, according to the LGA. In addition, central London has been particularly impacted by the Covid pandemic, and many of the Council's regular additional income streams (promotions & filming, parking charges, and discretionary services) have substantially reduced during the pandemic. A number of local businesses have also left the borough or ceased trading as a result of the pandemic, leaving empty shop fronts in central London and consequently reduced business rates income for the Council. Officers are developing an investment strategy to meet our net zero carbon targets, but we have not yet fully ascertained how the entire climate programme will be funded, especially where carbon emissions lie outside of the Council's direct control. However, the Council did ringfence an initial £5 million to build our climate programme capacity, and this has remained set aside even after the Covid pandemic. column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster's housing stock contains a high proportion of historic properties, with about half of the borough's total housing stock having been built before 1900. Historic properties can be harder to retrofit and bring up to modern insulation standards, both due to planning constraints and to structural issues such as historic properties tending to have solid walls rather than cavity walls, and solid walls being more challenging to insulate. In addition, Westminster's dense urban characteristics means that there are limited opportunities to build new low-carbon developments. This means that many existing buildings will require deep retrofit measures, and where deep retrofit is not technically feasible, buildings will need to be redeveloped instead, involving the challenges of demolition and relocation of existing residents. Given that 86% of Westminster's overall GHG emissions come from the built environment, the limited opportunities for new development and the historic nature of the existing stock are some of the biggest challenges that the city faces in overcoming and adapting to climate change.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster has a very high cost of living: the average mean household income in Westminster is £52,199, yet the median house price was £1,054,400 in 2017. This is nearly two times higher than London as a whole, and almost five times higher than that of the UK. Westminster also has a high proportion of private renters (40% of the total resident population), and private rental prices are more than £3,000 a month. This is a challenge as it means that many residents have little disposable income to invest in improving the energy efficiency of their properties through retrofit, or purchasing electric vehicles rather than petrol/diesel ones. This will make it more difficult to achieve our net carbon zero goals by 2040.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The Council has strong political support for action on climate change across both the majority (Labour) and minority (Conservative) parties that currently have representation amongst Councillors. A climate emergency was declared at Full Council in September 2019 and although the council had a change of political administration in May 2022 the new Cabinet Members have continued to show strong support for action on climate change in spite of the cost of living crisis and the ongoing Covid pandemic. Furthermore, the Council has a robust climate action governance system in place, consisting of monthly officer meetings where internal departments are held to account on their actions to reduce the Council's own emissions, as well as quarterly meetings of a Climate Leadership Group which is led by the Leader of the Council and sets the high-level strategic agenda for action on climate change. The Climate Emergency team are regularly asked to present on progress to the Council's political Cabinet, to statutory Scrutiny Committees, and directly to the Leader of the Council, which ensures that officers continue to pursue high levels of ambition.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster has a highly transient population, with approximately one-fifth of the resident population moving into or out of the borough every year. This is partly due to high numbers of students and foreign nationals being amongst the resident population. The churn is particularly noticeable in the private rented sector, where it is estimated that only 45% of renters stay in Westminster for more than one year. Having a highly transient population raises challenges around getting residents engaged in the Westminster's work to tackle climate change, as many of the borough's short-term residents will not feel a strong connection to Westminster as a place. These residents will be harder to engage with through local channels on our developing Climate Action Plan.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Westminster has high levels of inequality, as it contains some of the wealthiest areas of the UK as well as some of the most deprived. This inequality is particularly noticeable around health outcomes. Depending on where residents live in Westminster, life expectancy varies for men by 18 years between the most and least deprived parts of the borough, and for women the gap is 9 years. This is the fourth highest gap in England. The inequalities of 'healthy' life expectancy are even wider. Data shows that in the more deprived areas, people are living a greater proportion of their lives in poor health. In Westminster, this gap in healthy life expectancy between the most and least deprived areas is 20 years for men and 19 years for women. This data was gathered pre-Covid, and it is likely that the pandemic has only exacerbated this health inequality trend. This raises challenges with regards to climate change mitigation and adaptation. Residents who are living in poor health or caring for someone in poor health are more at risk from the impacts of climate change such as the increased prevalence of heatwaves. Furthermore, the range of health outcomes amongst Westminster residents means that a 'one size fits all' approach to climate change adaption will not be as effective, and officers will need to be very sensitive to the needs of individual communities when designing mitigation and adaptation solutions.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: Nanaimo is a hilly coastal community on Vancouver Island. The City's land use pattern constrained by Mount Benson to the west and the ocean (Salish Sea) to the east. The City's long and spread out land use pattern along with the hilly terrain can make active transportation somewhat challenging and limits land use planning options for a compact, walkable community. Historically low density land use patterns have further increased these challenges. As a coastal city Nanaimo is vulnerable to the impacts of sea level rise and storm surges; however, the City's elevated terrain and location on the more protected east side of Vancouver Island help minimizes this risk. The City's Sea Level Rise Study has identified a few low lying areas of the City as vulnerable to sea level rise including the downtown core and Duke Point Industrial Park while other areas are protected by steeper terrain. However, some of those areas of steep terrain are vulnerable to coastal erosion. The impacts of erosion are expected to increase due to rising sea levels and an increase in ocean storm events. The City's steep terrain also reduces local flooding, due to the high banks of most local rivers. Traditionally, flooding is most common along the estuary of the Nanaimo River which is just outside the City boundary but does include land reserved for the Snuneymuxw First Nation.

The CCR Risk Assessment has identified the following international dimensions climate change high risks; Risks to UK food availability, safety, and quality from climate change overseas. Risks to the UK from international violent conflict resulting from climate change overseas Risks to international law and governance from climate change overseas that will impact the UK. Risks associated with international trade routes. Risk to UK public health from climate change overseas. Systemic risk arising from the amplification of named risks cascading across sectors and borders. The Advice Report for CCRA3 sets out how most products, including food, finished goods, components and materials, have complex - often international - supply chains. Extreme weather is already causing supply chain disruption and exposure to climate hazards is set to increase. Climate hazards can affect the supply of food, goods and vital services, as well as the infrastructure and routes by which these are transported. Adaptation actions involve the provision of better information, diversification of supply chain risks and building better capacity to manage, share and transfer risk. It highlights that there is an important role for new technology and infrastructure. The government understands that the potential for cascading risks is growing through a more inter-connected world, where risks can spread across sectors and in doing so lead to system-wide consequences. 

The Integrated Review has committed the government to publish a Resilience Strategy which will detail how the UK can improve its resilience to the effects of a wide range of risks, including climate change impacts. By 2030, the government aims to have improved its ability to assess and understand the risks we face. In 2024, Welsh Government published their own climate adaptation strategy, setting out high level cross-sector adaptation plans for Wales, https://www.gov.wales/climate-adaptation-strategy-wales-2024 however, in April 2025, the Climate Change Committee Progress in adapting to climate change: 2025 report to Parliament highlighted the UK's preparations for climate change are inadequate and adaptation progress is either too slow, has stalled, or is heading in the wrong direction.

column16: Uno de los principales desafíos que enfrenta el GAD de Manta para realizar una planificación adecuada radica en su posición geográfica y las condiciones particulares del territorio. Manta, al ser una ciudad costera, está expuesta a fenómenos naturales como la erosión marina, inundaciones, y marejadas, que afectan no solo a la infraestructura sino también a la habitabilidad de ciertas zonas. Estos riesgos se ven incrementados por el cambio climático, que intensifica la frecuencia e intensidad de los eventos extremos, como las lluvias torrenciales o sequías prolongadas, complicando la planificación a largo plazo.\n\nAdemás, la expansión urbana acelerada de Manta ha puesto presión sobre los recursos naturales, especialmente el agua, y ha generado una demanda creciente de servicios básicos e infraestructura resiliente. El terreno accidentado y las variaciones topográficas también dificultan la creación de un sistema de drenaje eficiente, aumentando el riesgo de inundaciones en temporadas lluviosas.

La regulación ambiental de tierras, como los Acuerdos de Uso y Conservación de Suelo (ACUS), sería una herramienta clave para evitar la expansión descontrolada de urbanizaciones y el llenado de quebradas naturales en Manta. Estas regulaciones permitirían establecer límites claros sobre el uso del suelo, protegiendo áreas de alto valor ecológico y evitando que zonas destinadas a la conservación, como las quebradas y humedales, sean rellenadas o modificadas para el desarrollo urbano.

Implementar ACUS ayudaría a:

Preservar los ecosistemas naturales: Las quebradas y zonas verdes desempeñan un papel crucial en la regulación del ciclo del agua, la prevención de inundaciones y la conservación de la biodiversidad. Al regular el uso del suelo, se evitaría que estas áreas sean convertidas en urbanizaciones, protegiendo su función ecológica.

Frenar la expansión urbana desordenada: Las normativas más estrictas sobre el uso de la tierra reducirían la presión para desarrollar áreas fuera del plan urbano establecido, promoviendo un crecimiento planificado y sostenible que respete los ecosistemas frágiles.

Promover una planificación urbana más sostenible: Con el uso de ACUS, el GAD de Manta podría guiar el desarrollo hacia zonas apropiadas para la expansión urbana, evitando los impactos ambientales negativos que resultan de la construcción en áreas inadecuadas, como las quebradas.

Facilitar la recuperación y protección de áreas vulnerables: Las regulaciones ayudarían a restaurar áreas previamente dañadas y evitar que futuras intervenciones destructivas continúen degradando el entorno natural.

En resumen, la aplicación de regulaciones ambientales como los ACUS permitiría proteger de manera más efectiva los ecosistemas clave de Manta, promoviendo un desarrollo urbano que respete los límites ecológicos del territorio y garantice un uso sostenible del suelo a largo plazo.

Se ha establecido la necesidad de avanzar hacia definiciones de pobreza más amplias, claras e integrales y que, al mismo tiempo, permitan diseñar y validar métodos de medición pertinentes que den cuenta de la multidimensionalidad del fenómeno.Tradicionalmente, la pobreza en Chile ha sido medida a partir del ingreso total per cápita de los hogares, empleando una metodología que se encontraba vigente desde 1990, es decir, no actualizada en 25 años, existiendo consenso en que esta medición tradicional ya no daba cuenta de la situación de pobreza en que viven muchas familias. Una nueva mirada de este concepto ha sido desarrollada últimamente, entregando al país nuevas metodologías y mediciones que nos permiten entender la pobreza desde dos ángulos complementarios: la pobreza por ingresos y la pobreza multidimensional. Algunos datos sobre la Pobreza en Renca:➢ Porcentaje de personas en situación de pobreza por ingresos en el año 2020 de 10,2%, uno de los más altos de la Región Metropolitana.➢ Porcentaje de personas en situación de pobreza multidimensional, CASEN 2017: 24,52%.Finalmente, cabe destacar que durante el 2022, el departamento social de la Municipalidad, entregó un total de 28.622 ayudas sociales a los vecinos y vecinas que lo requirieron, los que en gran medida, intentan responder a las necesidades derivadas de la pobreza en la comuna.

column16: The East Central Florida region encompasses 8 counties, including 78 cities and towns. Each of these jurisdictions encounters its own government capacity challenges. Capability, administrative, budget/funding, and leadership barriers can hinder the ability of a government entity to address climate change adaptation and/or mitigation efforts. Moreover, depending on leadership stance and willingness, the connection between community-facing shocks and stressors like climate change might be overlooked or dismissed. These government capacity challenges become more prominent when working to build collaboration across jurisdictions and as a region due to the scale of work, as is the case for the East Central Florida Regional Resilience Collaborative. One of the collaborative goals is to assist in expanding the capability and capacity of local governments. Each project is designed to create interdepartmental opportunities, provide training by experts, and learn with a peer group within the region. The advisory committees with subject matter focus provide opportunity for each partner to engage and lean on the empirical expertise within the network. The collaborative provides leadership through targets and goals for implementation that each local government can point toward as they develop their pathway forward that makes the most sense within the political climate of their jurisdiction.

La educación ambiental constituye una herramienta esencial y estratégica para enfrentar los desafíos que impone la actual crisis climática. Una ciudadanía informada, consciente y participativa es clave para promover procesos de adaptación, mitigación y resiliencia frente a los efectos del cambio climático a nivel local y global.

Desde nuestra administración municipal, entendemos que el desarrollo sostenible no puede alcanzarse sin un componente educativo sólido, transversal e inclusivo. Por ello, la educación ambiental se consolida como un pilar fundamental de nuestra gestión, orientando políticas, programas y acciones territoriales que promuevan una transformación cultural hacia modelos de vida más sostenibles.

En ese sentido, se vienen impulsando diversas estrategias y gestiones con el objetivo de diseñar e implementar un Plan Municipal de Educación Ambiental Integral, que abarque todos los estratos sociales y grupos etarios. Este plan tiene como propósito:

Fomentar el conocimiento y comprensión del cambio climático, sus causas y consecuencias.

Promover la participación activa de la comunidad en acciones concretas de cuidado ambiental.

Fortalecer capacidades locales para la adaptación a fenómenos extremos como sequías, inundaciones, incendios forestales y olas de calor.

Integrar la dimensión ambiental en el sistema educativo formal, no formal e informal.

Generar alianzas con instituciones educativas, organizaciones sociales, actores comunitarios y el sector privado para ampliar el alcance de las iniciativas educativas.

Asimismo, se está trabajando en la generación de materiales didácticos, jornadas de sensibilización, talleres comunitarios, campañas informativas y programas de formación docente, entre otras acciones.

Public organisations are operating in a backdrop of ever-increasing resource and funding constraints, which are often hindering adaptation progress, and require transformation to keep pace with the increasing frequency and pressures of climate change. The Powys CCRA contextualisation survey completed with PSB members (see approach to the CCRA for further details) highlights significant limitations in organisational planning and preparedness for climate risks, with barriers around funding constraints, skills and capacity issues, and difficulties incorporating data into strategic and corporate planning. 
While emergency response remains vital, over-reliance on reactive strategies can strain resources and lead to higher economic, social, and environmental costs. Public Health Wales' Impact Assessment stresses the need to shift beyond responses to individual episodes, but towards long-term preventative adaptation. To support this transition, policies and procedures must actively support, rather than hinder, climate adaptation and avoid maladaptation. 
Strengthening institutional adaptive (coping) capacity of PSB member organisations, by making use of existing resources to adapt to climate risks and ensure continuity in service delivery, even in the face of increasingly complex climate impacts is critical. This means embedding climate risk into decision-making processes which inform organisational and strategic planning levels. Whilst strengthening staff capacity, data sharing, financing options for adaptation, and fostering partnership approaches across sectors.

column11: Identify and describe the most significant factors impacting on your jurisdiction's ability to adapt to climate change and indicate how those factors either support or challenge this ability.
column16: The budgetary capacity of the municipality of Katerini poses significant challenges to its adaptive capacity to climate change. Limited financial resources hinder the municipality's ability to invest in essential infrastructure upgrades and maintenance, leaving the city vulnerable to extreme weather events. This financial constraint prevents the implementation of necessary flood defenses, stormwater management systems, and resilient public buildings, increasing the risk of infrastructure failures during climate-related disasters. Moreover, the restricted budget affects the municipality's ability to conduct comprehensive climate risk assessments and develop effective adaptation plans. Without sufficient funding, Katerini struggles to acquire the necessary data and expertise required for informed decision-making. The lack of specialized staff further exacerbates the problem, as there are fewer experts available to address complex climate issues. Community engagement and public awareness campaigns are also compromised due to budget constraints. Educating the public about climate risks and promoting adaptive behaviors are crucial for building community resilience. However, limited funds restrict the scope and reach of these initiatives, resulting in lower public participation and awareness. Additionally, the municipality faces challenges in implementing and enforcing regulatory measures that promote climate resilience. Budget limitations lead to weak enforcement of building codes and zoning laws, delaying the adaptation process. Emergency preparedness and response efforts are similarly affected, as the municipality lacks the resources for adequate planning, training, and equipment. Furthermore, accessing external funding is often contingent on the availability of matching funds from the municipality. Katerini's limited budget hampers its ability to leverage national or EU grants, missing out on crucial financial support. Administrative capacity to apply for and manage such grants is also constrained, reducing opportunities for external funding. Finally, the municipality must balance climate adaptation with other pressing needs, such as healthcare and education. The constrained budget forces difficult trade-offs, often prioritizing short-term needs over long-term climate resilience investments.

column16:
Environmental conditions in Athienou both support and challenge the Municipality's adaptive capacity. On the one hand, Athienou is an agricultural community with long-standing experience in managing scarce resources under semi-arid conditions. Farmers have developed traditional practices to cope with water scarcity and extreme heat, which provides a basis of knowledge and resilience that can support adaptation. The relatively small geographic area of the Municipality also facilitates closer monitoring of environmental changes and targeted implementation of adaptation measures.

On the other hand, current and projected environmental conditions present significant challenges. Rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves increase health risks for residents and raise the likelihood of wildfires. Prolonged droughts threaten agriculture, livestock, and water supply, while also increasing the risk of land degradation and desertification. Intense rainfall events occurring within short periods create risks of localized flooding, especially where drainage infrastructure is limited. Loss of biodiversity and soil degradation further reduce the natural resilience of ecosystems, making it harder to rely on environmental assets for adaptation.

In summary, while Athienou's agricultural heritage and traditional knowledge provide some capacity to adapt to harsh conditions, the intensifying impacts of climate change—heat stress, drought, extreme rainfall, and ecosystem degradation—pose serious challenges that require strengthened adaptive measures and sustained support from higher levels of government.

Whilst there have been efforts to modernise many of these systems, they remain piecemeal with systems increasingly reliant on parts of the infrastructure that are over a hundred years old and reaching the end of their intended design life. The requirement to upgrade these systems does introduce the opportunity to make them fit for purpose, but until they are upgraded there is an increased risk of failure due to climate impacts. Food in the UK is 40% imported, with UK food and drink exports annually exceeding £20bn. This combination makes food infrastructure affecting the Square Mile vulnerable to national and international shocks and stresses, which may include weather-related shifts in agricultural production, geopolitical crises and events, legislation gaps and volatile food prices. The elderly are most exposed because they often have accessibly/mobility issues that will restrict the distance they can travel to access stores, therefore they are most affected when availability is limited. The requirements associated with historic and listed status, such as preserving architectural integrity, materials, and façades, place constraints on introducing energy efficiency measures and climate resilience adaptations. For example, the installation of double glazing, external insulation, or rooftop solar panels is often restricted, while the need for specialist materials and skills increases costs and complexity. To combat this, the City Corporation developed a Heritage Buildings Retrofit Toolkit in 2024, to address challenges related to adapting historic and listed buildings, providing tailored best-practice retrofit guidance to building owners and operators. \n

For example, urban greening interventions including tree planting - root systems and soil volumes cannot be accommodated without risking damage to vital system- which therefore affects the extent to which we can increase nature-based shading in the public realm and lower street temperatures in instances of extreme heat.

column16: Migration is one of the fundamental dynamics transforming Çorlu's social, economic, and environmental structure, creating both supportive and challenging effects on its capacity to adapt to climate change. In particular, increased internal migration, industrial mobility, and irregular population growth in recent years have increased demand for municipal services, placing serious pressure on the city's infrastructure systems and social services. This situation stands out as one of the most important factors challenging Çorlu's capacity to adapt to climate change. With increasing migration, housing demand, water consumption, waste production, and transportation needs have risen; existing green spaces have decreased, the urban heat island effect has grown, and disaster risks have become more fragile. In addition, the fact that a significant portion of the migrant population consists of low-income, socially unprotected, and vulnerable groups has deepened inequalities in access to health services, clean water, and resilient housing. This has made the fair and inclusive practices required for climate adaptation more complex and costly. On the other hand, migration also offers some opportunities that support the capacity for adaptation. In particular, the increase in the young and working-age population has increased the potential for participation in climate-friendly projects implemented by the municipality in areas such as green employment, environmental education, recycling, and energy efficiency, thanks to the expansion of human resources. In addition, the cultural diversity of the immigrant population can facilitate the spread of social awareness campaigns on climate change to different segments of society and the diversification of participation mechanisms at the local level. column16: Budget capacity is one of the determining factors in local governments' climate change adaptation processes, and for Çorlu Municipality, this element is both an important constraint and an area requiring strategic guidance. Çorlu's rapidly growing population, developing industry, and increasing infrastructure needs are increasing pressure on municipal resources, making it difficult to allocate sufficient budget to long-term, multi-sectoral, and costly intervention areas such as climate adaptation. For example, critical adaptation measures such as green infrastructure investments, the establishment of flood and drought-resistant systems, energy efficiency projects, and the reduction of social vulnerabilities typically require high initial costs. However, since Çorlu Municipality's current budget necessitates prioritizing essential service areas (cleaning, transportation, infrastructure maintenance, etc.), climate adaptation is often relegated to a secondary priority. While this situation stands out as a factor limiting adaptation capacity, it also encourages the municipality to seek creative and efficient ways to use resources. For example, applying for EU-supported grant programs, developing partnerships with institutions such as UNDP and TÜBİTAK, establishing public-private partnerships with the private sector, and seeking access to green financing tools (carbon credits, climate bonds, etc.) enable Çorlu to take steps in the field of climate adaptation despite its limited budget. column16:
Quang Binh Province faces a severe housing crisis driven by frequent natural disasters, especially typhoons and floods. This situation presents a profound challenge to the adaptive capacity of the provincial government, testing its governance, financial resources, and planning capabilities.

The scale of unsafe housing in Quang Binh creates an immense burden. A large portion of the population, particularly poor and near-poor households, lives in structures unable to withstand natural disasters. The recurring cycle of destruction and reconstruction depletes public finances and diverts resources from long-term development goals.

The provincial government's efforts to support the construction of thousands of storm- and flood-resilient homes, often in collaboration with international partners like the UNDP, have yielded positive results. However, implementation has exposed significant challenges to the jurisdiction's administrative capacity. Issues such as delays in land-use planning, inaccurate beneficiary verification, and escalating material costs have hindered the effectiveness of these programs.

Financially, the cost of building or retrofitting resilient housing is substantial. The province's budget, supplemented by external aid, is insufficient to meet the overwhelming need. At the same time, the economic vulnerability of many households makes them entirely dependent on external support, placing further pressure on the government.

Ultimately, the housing challenge is deeply intertwined with socio-economic factors. High poverty rates and a lack of sustainable livelihoods exacerbate the impacts of disasters. Therefore, the government's adaptive capacity depends not only on building physical infrastructure but also on addressing these root social issues.

To overcome this challenge, Quang Binh requires a more comprehensive strategy to enhance its adaptive capacity. This includes institutional reforms to streamline procedures, diversifying sustainable financial mechanisms (such as public-private partnerships), and strengthening the role of local communities in disaster risk reduction. Integrating safe housing policies into broader socio-economic development plans is the key to building a more resilient and secure future for its residents.
